paragraphs.text: He proclaims Christ's divinity as though the world did not know it.

And why does he claim for himself what is common to all? Because many believed, both those who had seen the Lord and those who had not, but Paul is called from heaven: "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" He also has something more than the other apostles. The Lord himself called Peter, James, John and those with them and had them as disciples, but he did not at once make them or name them apostles; Paul, however, he called and brought into the apostleship at one and the same time.
And that the gospel is preached by the will of the Father.

He said "his prophets" because there are also prophets of idols, and by this phrase he distinguishes prophets from prophets and gospel from gospels. For there are many announcements of good news, but they are mortal and temporary, whereas the gospel of Christ promises the enjoyment of eternal goods "in the holy scriptures." So the prophets too are his, and not another god's, but those of the Father of Christ.
And "to the saints" is not said idly. Since many are called but few are chosen, and not all persevered in their calling, he says it so as not to throw what is holy to the dogs.

According to the heretics: if Christ is Lord and God is our Father, then the Father too will be a servant of Christ, for as the Son is, so is the Father. But that is not how things are. He said "our Father" to show grace, and "the Lord Jesus" so that they would not grow proud, as though they too were sons of God, and either pull down the Son's glory or raise themselves above their nature.

He called God "Father" because he judges no one, and the Son "Lord" because he is the judge. He says "Father" to show his care for us, and he calls the Son "Lord" so that we may know that we are called sons by God's goodness, while Jesus himself, being true God by nature, is our Lord.

And again, since many were hurrying to Rome for merely human reasons, he shows his longing, and by the addition shows that it is a pious one. He presents himself as longing for the Romans, perhaps because the faith of the Romans counted for more, since it became an encouragement to everyone under their rule.
That God is truly God, whereas the idols they worshipped are falsely called gods.
He does not mention such shameful conduct idly, but because he had heard that in Rome there was also prostitution of males.

By "the decree of God" he means his just recompense, which he pays back to each according to what each deserves. So this is what he says: even though people know from their natural understanding that wrongdoers are bound to be punished by God, they still do not keep away from the worst deeds, and, most dreadful of all, they even approve of those who do them. So "the decree of God" he says is this very thing, that those who do such things deserve death; or else he means simply God's justice, or the commandments, or the Mosaic law, which commands this clearly and severely, judging those who do such things worthy of death. "Therefore you are without excuse, O man, every one of you who judges; for in judging another you condemn yourself, since you who judge do the same things."

By "storing up" he showed that sins gathered up little by little become, through the patience of the judge, an increase of punishment for those whose sickness is incurable. He does not say that God is angry in order to charge God with passion; rather, he borrows the usage of human beings to speak about God's judgment, which in the present life is hidden and unseen, being reserved for the time of judgment. Here too God orders things wisely, not according to the strict order of justice, since the impious do not notice even when they are treated well now, and the righteous, tested by the hardships of life, did not change their pious way of living. Not knowing this, some are scandalized and say that nothing is governed by providence, supposing that God does not watch over human affairs. But when the appointed time of recompense comes, then the light of God's righteous judgment is revealed and shines out, and each receives what the life he has lived deserves. So by the image of "the day of wrath" he taught that now is not the time for punishment, or wrath, or God's righteous judgment.

Just as what comes from selfish ambition is inexcusable, so too is the case of one who perpetrates evil, as distinct from one who merely does it. For a person may do evil while struggling against it and being overcome, but perpetrating it belongs to the deliberate and diligent practice of evil.

In the case of evil he assigned condemnation, not without qualification, but to those who perpetrate it; in the case of good he assigned glory, and not only to those who carry it through, so that by both God's goodness might be shown: that he condemns not simply those who do evil but those who perpetrate it, and that he honors even those who simply do good.
He rightly says here "the Jew first" and then "the Greek"; for those who are nearer to the master are counted worthy of both rebukes and honors beyond the others.

"What advantage then do we hold? For we have already charged both Jews and Greeks," and so on. This is said elliptically. After "What advantage then do we hold?" the natural thing would have been to add "the righteousness that comes from faith," which he does say as he goes on: "the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ." What advantage then do we hold? The righteousness that comes from faith; for we have already charged both Jews and Greeks. How did he charge them? By convicting the Greeks of corrupting their natural knowledge, where he said, "For God has shown it to them. For his invisible attributes have been clearly seen since the creation of the world, being understood through the things he has made," and "because, though they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks"; and by convicting the Jews of transgressing the law, in the words "You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God by transgressing the law?" Having shown that in the one case nature had failed, and in the other both nature and the law, he then logically introduces the grace that comes from the gospel and says, in effect: What advantage, what special privilege, do we have from grace? Faith, which brings about righteousness through Jesus Christ.

Nowhere does he say that all were impious, but that all "sinned": the common condition of sin, not of impiety. And one who falls short, having something that is lacking, seeks what is missing. The Jews had the law, but they lacked the perfection that grace brings.

God was forbearing in order to show his own righteousness. Had he proceeded against them, he would certainly have destroyed them, and if he had destroyed them, there would have been no one to be saved. But since he bore with them even as their sins piled up, he showed that he had borne with them earlier because he wished not only to free them from their sins but also to justify them. So, having allowed them to sin, he granted forgiveness all at once. We call God righteous either because he repays or because he grants righteousness. That by which I am justified, then, is God's righteousness, since it comes not from my works but from the grace of the one who justifies.

Circumcision was given for these three reasons: to be a sign of faith, a mark identifying the race of Abraham, and a symbol and figure of a pure and chaste way of life. So it was not given as something that produces righteousness, but as a seal and sign of the righteousness that Abraham had from faith.

He says that the righteous will be heirs of the world because, once the impious have been removed and handed over to punishment on the day of judgment, the righteous will possess the whole remaining world, renewed, and both heavenly and earthly goods will be theirs.
"In the presence of him whom he believed": that is, before the face of God, whom he believed.
Against the hope that his own nature offered, in hope of the power of the one who made the promise. And "so shall your offspring be" refers not only to their number but also to their splendor.

By saying "he was strengthened" he shows that faith is achieved with great toil, strength of soul and effort. And how was he strengthened? "Giving glory to God," he says; that is, not inquiring curiously how this could come about, but believing at once and praising God as his benefactor, as though he had already given what he had promised.

Do you see how he draws a distinction here too? For sin and righteousness he uses "many", since not all who lived before the law sinned, nor did all who are under grace act righteously, for many are called but few are chosen; but for bodily death and bodily resurrection he says "all" and "all".
Because when we are baptized we confess that we have died to the world and renounce sin and the devil.
To live in newness is to begin a new and fresh life, having put off the old life spent in sins; for regeneration too announces the conduct of a new and fresh life.
Those who live according to the old man have a body of sin, exposed to the devil's schemes; but those who live according to the

new man, our Lord Jesus, have a body of righteousness, since they are members of the Lord. So, although the devil incites people to sin, now that he has been defeated through Christ and the flesh of the Word has been nailed to the cross, the evil one has been cast out, and those who wish to are now free. For whoever has died in the sense that baptism means has died to the world, and has been justified and released from punishment, having been set free from sin.

It was not by commanding us not to sin that the law gave occasion for stumbling, but by allowing indulgence to the passions. Giving the passions a pretext, then, was not the law's aim; what happened belonged to the dispensation under which it was given at that time. I mean that eating and drinking were at work in our members (for desire stirs even in those who fast), but they are not at work so as to bear fruit for death. That is why Moses is described as a ministry of death: because the law was a burden, and what it intended it did not achieve, while what it did not want it brought about.

The law, he says, is not evil, nor is it sin; but while it made sin known, it was unable to remove it, and so it gave sin an occasion to grow. And why was this, he asks? To show how great sin is, so as to show at the same time the surpassing greatness of grace. Sin was so strong, he says, that it prevailed all the more and grew stronger through the very things that forbade it. Just as a flame, when it is starting, is put out by anything at hand, but once it has blazed up further even the water meant to quench it makes it burn more, so the law exposed sin, which had taken hold of the whole world and was spreading over everyone, but could not quench it.

Because one who sinned in ignorance cannot be condemned; but the law, once given, showed sin for what it was and so gave sin its power. This is not an accusation against the law, but a reproof of the negligence of those who do not keep it. And just as sin is dead apart from the law, so too sin is dead when the law is kept.

By "law" he means the Mosaic law, and by "commandment" the one given to Adam in paradise: holy, because it taught what was right; just, because it rightly passed sentence on those who transgressed; and good, because it prepared life for those who kept it.

So, having contemplated in his mind the war waged through the body against the soul, and the man taken captive by it, he seeks a refuge of salvation and looks around for a deliverer who might transform this very body of death into a body of life. Then, as though the deliverer had been found and stood ready to grant the grace of salvation, he offers fitting thanks to God through Jesus Christ, through whom his deliverance from the enemy also came to him. He does not simply say, or pray, that he may be delivered from the body, but from the death that took hold of the body through sin: "the body of death". For he wants his body to be a body of life, not a body of death or a body of sin.
By "the Spirit of Christ" he meant the gifts of the new covenant.

Some say that the "spirit of slavery" is that of the evil one, but this is not so. Here he calls the law a spirit of slavery, and those under the law slaves. That is why they were afraid, as people liable to punishment if they stumbled, and this is a mark of slavery. But being permitted to call God Father because of the purity of one's life holds out hopes of adoption. And it is the same Spirit that was at work in both peoples, as a spirit of slavery and as a spirit of adoption, according to what was beneficial and fitting for the standing of each.

"Eager expectation" means intent watching for what is hoped for. It takes its name from the way someone who is waiting tilts his head forward and strains his eyes, as though he were about to see at any moment what he is waiting for.

Or "the image of the Son" stands for the Holy Spirit. For just as the Son is the exact image of the Father, so too the Spirit is the image of the Son. So all who have been counted worthy of the Holy Spirit and live spiritually are conformed to the Spirit, who is the image of the Son.

By these words he shows the boundless love that Christ has for us. He was not content to die for us, but he also intercedes with the Father on our behalf. And clearly he intercedes for the same things as when he lived among people in the flesh, for he asked the Father, saying, "I want them also to be where I am." For this [?] the Savior intercedes. Yet he does not intercede to inform the Father about our affairs, as though the Father did not know them, nor as though the Father were unwilling; for what the Father wills, the Son wills too. What, then, is the point of the pleading and intercession? The passage cuts off in advance the impiety of Sabellius that was to come, teaching that although the Trinity is one in substance, it is not one hypostasis. For the intercession shows that the one who asks is distinct from the one who is asked. It is not unfitting for the Son to ask and the Father to grant, so that a fitting order may be preserved between the two persons. Or would it not be unfitting for the Son, knowing the Father's mind, to forestall the Father's gift and bestow the grace by seizing it? In the same way, all things were indeed created through the Son, but by the will of the Father, so that throughout, proper sequence and fittingness may be preserved between the two persons. The passage therefore teaches us the unconfused order of Father and Son. And if you take the one who asks to be Christ in the flesh, the passage will seem much easier still to understand.

Having splendidly shown God's disposition toward us and the love of his Son, he goes on to teach what sort of people the grateful ought to be toward their benefactor: such that not even the most terrifying things can separate us from Christ.

Some think this is the solution, especially Asterius the Cappadocian, who understands it like this: You who contradict me, how do you contradict? Is it not from the freedom of your will? Are you not answering back to God? On this view Paul wants to show that God does not compel, even while he makes people righteous, for freedom remains with human beings. But this interpretation does not make sense, for he goes on: "Will what is molded say to the one who molded it, 'Why did you make me like this?'" That is not the language of someone showing that we are free, but quite the opposite. What, then, is the meaning? This is said for good measure; it is not offered as the solution. And what does "for good measure" mean? "But above all, who are you?" Let us suppose that we have no will and are not free: did God not have the authority to act as he wished? A potter shapes some vessels for honor and others for dishonor; does God not have the authority a potter has, to honor whom he wishes and punish whom he will? Having said this for good measure, he then gives the solution.

By "demonstration of wrath" he means that, being patient with human beings, God allows them, through their free will, to do what they wish. And by "vessels of wrath prepared for destruction" he means human beings who are under the sentence of death.

Some others, however, supplied "What do you know?" to complete "What if God, wishing to show his wrath" and so on, taking it as an ellipsis to be filled in from outside. And "with much patience" means: after much patience he brought on his wrath.

Christ is not a part of the law but the beginning of another life. So he is called the end of the law because he became the end of the law, that is, he brought it to a stop. He is the end of the law, then, in two senses: because he made use of it and because he brought it to a stop. And "for everyone who believes" means not only for the Jew but also for the Greek, not as though he were the end of the law for the Jew alone.

By mentioning the cultivated olive and the wild olive he showed that all have one nature, as with the olive tree, but not one choice, as with the wild and the cultivated tree. He calls "wild" what is estranged from the master and useless to him, and "cultivated" what bears fruit. By "grafting" he means being grafted into the faith of Abraham, whom he calls the root, and he says that the grafting gives life.

However, this is said elliptically, which is why it lacks a connecting word. What he means is this: by comparison with you, the Jews are shown to be enemies of God, since you who come from the Gentiles believed, while those who ought to have believed before everyone else were hardened in heart. In this respect they are enemies of God, but they are beloved for the sake of their fathers; in their honor God will show kindness to their descendants and will regard them as beloved once they have believed and shown a way of life that can save them.

The present state of the world urges human beings toward luxury and pleasure. Whoever renounces this "form" will move himself into a different and unfamiliar way of life. Having become a new man, he is transformed from one thing into another.

Having said earlier that God measures out the measure of faith, he uses the illustration that follows both to defend the giver and to persuade anyone with a lesser gift not to be grieved. For however lowly a part of the body may be, it is useful to the whole, and the great and the small are joined together into one body; this is the conclusion drawn from what came before, that we are members of one another. "Having different gifts" stands for "each one, however, having different gifts." "He who gives, with simplicity": this is what the Lord says: "Give to everyone who asks you," without inquiring whether the person is good or bad, or to whom you are giving. For such scrupulousness often keeps us from giving to those to whom we ought to give, since our suspicions are often mistaken.

It is right to be subject to kings who devote themselves to serving God's will, unless perhaps persecution is at issue. For he has already taught about enduring everything for the faith, saying, "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?" and so on. He does not allow us to submit even to angels or principalities when it leads to lawlessness; how then could he advise us to obey human authorities that use force to make us turn away from God? But someone may say: If kingdoms are established by God, how is it that they sometimes make war even on the God-fearing? To such people it must be said that, although persecution seems very grievous to most, one must consider how much good it does them. God does not allow such things for no reason, but so that the virtues of the righteous may shine out and the vices of those in power may be exposed. Most important of all, it is then that those who put on the outward appearance of piety while being impious are exposed, and the genuine lovers of piety, finding in the time of persecution an occasion to win distinction, will show the fruit of their virtuous struggle. So, indeed, God also said to Job: "Do you think I have dealt with you for any other reason than that you might be shown to be righteous?"

Since love is such a thing, it naturally carries many advantages within it. One who loves does not commit adultery, does not murder, does nothing else that is forbidden, so that whoever has love has in this way fulfilled the whole law at once through love.

Fulfill the work of love, he says, knowing that the time is pressing and demands virtue. "Now our salvation is nearer than when we believed": that is, now that we know which works are more profitable, being saved has become easier than when we were still being instructed in the word of faith as catechumens. For at the moment we believed in Christ we did not also have an exact grasp of what we must do, but now we know it exactly.
The servant of Christ, whom Christ has accepted, is a stranger to the law. Who are you, then, to judge by the law one who is a stranger to the law?
"Through him": that is, through God.
Not as though he were refusing fellowship with the other apostles, but because he judged it grasping and unjust to snatch the glory of other people's labors.
That is, to use prudence so as not to be wronged by others, and innocence so as not to scheme against others.
He did not put this first for no reason, but to show that it is God's will that all should be named after Christ, and that there should be apostles.
He ranks him with himself as someone known to the Corinthians, and at the same time he checks the conceit of those who were puffed up about eloquence.
He mends the division that had wrongly arisen, calling them one church, and God's church. And he adds "in Christ Jesus", not "in So-and-so and So-and-so".

We should notice how often, in a few words, he mentions Christ Jesus, teaching from the very opening that it is right to be named after no one but our Lord Jesus Christ, and healing the wound caused by the divisions over different names through his constant mention of Jesus Christ. "To those sanctified in Christ Jesus." No human being sanctified you, he says, but God in Christ.

For if you call upon a man, he says, take your name from him; but if you call upon Jesus Christ, take your name from the one you call upon. And "with all who call upon" is well said; for not you alone, but all believers everywhere call upon Christ and are named after him, not after human beings. So do not make yourselves strange by introducing, alone among them, an impious novelty. And he did not say "with all who name the name" but "with all who call upon", showing that the Son of God is God, for it is God that one calls upon. "In every place, theirs and ours." If every place calls upon Jesus Christ, imitate the many, and do not, alone of all, do something strange that sets you apart from the rest. And "theirs and ours" is attached to "Lord", meaning: both we who write and you who receive the letter have one Christ Jesus.
Take your name from him from whom you have grace and peace. For the theses of these, taken up even before the proof and the training of the contests, [?] to the question at hand.
This too contributes no less to correcting the matters at hand. For if grace comes from our Lord Jesus Christ and not from men, it is fitting, he says, to be named after him.

He keeps to the same point. For if wealth comes from him, if knowledge comes from him, why do you take for yourselves the name of one man as your teacher, of another as the one who baptized you, of another as your leader, and of yet another as your provider? That is why, further on, he says: "What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?" "In all speech." Since there is a word of wisdom and a word of knowledge and many words of spiritual gifts, he therefore says, "in all speech and all knowledge." And since there are also many kinds of knowledge, he says "and all knowledge." The letter was written to Greeks, who had not received the Old and the New together, and who were acquiring knowledge from both sides. "Just as the testimony of Christ was confirmed among you."

Those who still need confirming are not yet complete. So he has shown that they need correction: he gives thanks for what they have received, but corrects them for what they have failed to fulfil. "God is faithful, through whom you were called." Since he had said, "God will confirm you," he added, "God is faithful" (for the God who is able to grant these things is true), "through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son": not into fellowship with a man, but into the fellowship of his Son. Why then do you give up being named after the Son into whose fellowship you were called, and take your names from men? Note too that "through whom" is used of the Father, not only of the Son. Nor is it any lowering of the Father that we are called through him into the fellowship of his Son. When it is written in Romans that all things are through him and from him and to him, God does not thereby become greater than himself because of "from whom" and less than himself because of "through whom." Just as these expressions, applied to the same person, do not make him both less and greater than himself, so neither does "through whom," when said of the Son, make him lesser.

When he came to the contest itself, to persuade them not to be named after men, he mentions the name of Jesus Christ, after whom everyone ought to be called, right from the beginning of the struggle. What is said here is not about doctrines, nor does he blame them over doctrine. It is about what we mentioned before, as what follows shows.

Does Christ have co-heirs, he says, with whom he has divided you believers among them? For he did not say, "Was Christ divided?" but "Has Christ shared you out?" And what follows shows this, for he says: "Was Paul crucified for us?" It was Christ who died for the salvation of the world, and none of us.

From this he shows that some wanted to be named after the one who had baptized them. This good thing, which the Saviour commanded and which brings salvation, became a burden to me, he says, if you were going to be called after me because I baptized you. But how are we to understand "Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel"? Even someone who is not an apostle baptizes, while few held the dignity of apostleship, and no one could be baptized without first having the gospel preached to them [and being baptized]. So he says, "I was sent to preach the gospel," for this is the primary thing, not baptizing. The word "primarily" is therefore understood here: "I was not primarily sent to baptize." So too elsewhere, when he says, "Is it for oxen that God cares?", it is not that he does not care. In the law Moses speaks about oxen, really meaning the animals that serve farmers. David also says, "Men and beasts you will save, O Lord, as you have multiplied your mercy, O God." And Solomon says, "The righteous man has pity on the lives of his beasts"; how much more, then, does God? So what does he mean? That God does not care primarily for oxen. Here too the expression is elliptical, as with "Christ did not send me to baptize."

As he passes to another charge and moves on to another correction, without entirely setting aside the first, he uses an introduction for the second. "Christ did not send me to baptize" belonged to the first charge, that each of you says, "I belong to Paul," "I to Apollos," while "not with wisdom of speech" begins another matter. So he has made "to preach the gospel" the end of the first matter and the beginning of the second. "So that the cross of Christ may not be emptied." For if the preaching is credited to human intelligence and education, the power of the cross is not shown.

"The word of the cross." He does not mean the spoken word or its utterance, but its power. The deed looks weak, but when its cause is examined it proves to be a great mystery. "But to us who are being saved it is the power of God." Since some want to take "Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God" as referring to God the Word, we should note from this passage that he calls the word of the cross the power of God. "For it is written: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise." Although the apostle was trustworthy teaching on his own authority, since he had Christ speaking in him, he nevertheless also uses the testimony of the Old Testament, to give the disciples a stronger assurance. Having used the testimony "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise," he then goes on as though the point were agreed: "Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe?" The wise man belongs to the Greeks, the scribe to the Jews.

He mentions two kinds of wisdom. One is the harmony seen in created things; the other is the wisdom by which human beings, being rational, have understanding. Since, then, he says, we did not know God through the understanding we possess, nor through the wisdom seen in created things, God was pleased to save those who believe through the foolishness of preaching. What he says is profound, though it escapes those who merely skim past it, for in this way he shows God's power and supreme wisdom. The greatness and beauty of the world, he says, immeasurable and beyond reach as it is, did not persuade you to recognize God. Instead you abandoned the Maker and worshipped the very things through which you ought to have recognized their Maker. God, showing you the surpassing greatness of his power, enlightened the world through the admitted weakness of the cross: the very people whom creation had not persuaded but had even overawed.

To show how absurd it is for people to rely on eloquence and to imagine that they adorn piety with fine speaking, he says that one should not answer the Greeks who seek wisdom, nor even give signs to the Jews who ask for them. Yet signs belong to the Spirit, whereas wisdom of words belongs to outside learning. If it was not right to give even the wonders of the Spirit to those who asked for them, much less the products of outside wisdom (for one gives not to those who test but to those who ask in faith), then eloquence is cast out altogether, as a threat to the glory of the cross. "But we preach Christ crucified," and so on. Clearly he calls Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God with reference to the word of the cross, as above: "For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God." And what follows shows this more plainly. After saying, "but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God," he added, "because the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men." Who would say that "the weakness of God" refers to God the Word? "The foolishness of God" is said of Christ crucified. God the Word is powerful as the Father is, not as a power that is a part completing the Father's essence; and likewise he is wise. Visible creation could not accomplish it, nor could angels or archangels coming down from heaven, the patriarchs and prophets, the law given through Moses, or the voices that came to the people from the midst of the fire, because the will of the ungrateful would not allow it. Since what none of these could accomplish the foolishness of the cross did accomplish, Christ crucified is the power of God and the wisdom of God, more effective than the whole dispensation and more convincing than all creation. This too shows the power of the one who arranged and accomplished it, saving human beings by means of what seemed nothing and bringing them to faith in himself.

Since the Jews put the Spirit of God to the test, whereas [the Spirit's gifts] are to be granted to those who believe, and since one must not answer the Greeks who think they can adorn piety with eloquence, he then explains how the preaching seems to be foolishness. They seek signs and wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, the power and wisdom of God, and we promise salvation from the crucified one to those who believe.

It is not God the Word who should be called "the weakness of God," but the cross of Christ. For the Word is powerful as the Father is, not a power in the sense of a part completing the Father's essence. In the same way the Son is wise as the Father is. Angels, the law and the prophets could not accomplish it, because God respects the free choice of the ungrateful. But the apparent foolishness of the cross did accomplish it, and so Christ crucified is proclaimed as the power and wisdom of God: he has shown himself stronger and more effective, and has saved those who believe.
He added "according to the flesh" to set it in contrast with the Spirit, and he applies what follows in the same way to all alike.

"So that no flesh may boast before him": that is, so that they might not credit the success of the preaching to their own advantages. He said "flesh" and not "soul" to belittle human boasting. Why "before him" and not "before men"? Because boasting in our own advantages had been set up against boasting in God: what they should have credited to God, they credited to men. That is why he said "before him," for boasting done in the sight of the One who sees all things was impious. The whole subject shows that he did not say "before him" with reference to the Second Coming, for [?] he is addressing those who boast in eloquence and in baptizing and in certain other things.

"It is from him that you are." Everyone agrees that this refers to having been saved, not to creation, as he says elsewhere: "who were born not of blood nor of the will of the flesh but of God." If, then, we are from him, how can we boast in our own advantages? And "in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom and sanctification and redemption": it was not human wisdom that saved us, for that had gone astray, but he himself became wisdom for us, leading to the knowledge of God. It was not human intelligence that snatched us away, but Jesus crucified. It was not men who redeemed us. So let the boasting be in the one who saved, not in those who were saved.

I was always afraid that you would be puffed up by outside learning, and that is why I did not use persuasive wisdom. "In weakness," he says, meaning the weakness that came from persecutions (this is how he always speaks), "in weakness and in fear and in trembling": the weakness that came from being persecuted. I showed fear and trembling on your account, and was humble in every way, so that you might learn from this and not be puffed up.

Since he said "my speech," he did not want to seem to be offering its opposite, that is, eloquence. So he says, "and my preaching was not in persuasive words of wisdom," since there is a wisdom that belongs not to words but to divine knowledge, to the Spirit and to power. The Holy Spirit both supplies the word of wisdom and works wonders, and so he said, "in demonstration of the Spirit and of power." What is said is not yet a demonstration, but a wonder carries its own demonstration.
He shows that he did not preach relying on any human power either. He was in weakness and fear and trembling, and in conditions like these, since he was under persecution and affliction.

Had he merely spoken, he would have been no different from those who use wisdom and rely on their own eloquence. But by working miracles he showed the might of God, and the preaching came from there. So he rightly added: "but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might rest not on human wisdom but on the power of God."

That is, not among the eloquent but among those who are perfect in piety. He said "among the perfect," not "to the perfect," because whoever speaks to ordinary people often meets with contradiction. But whoever introduces the saving word among the perfect and pious does not so much speak as deposit the words in their souls and store them up there like treasure.

If it had been hidden, then clearly it was not for human reasoning to discover it; it truly belonged to God to reveal it. Instead of simply stating that they did not understand, he gives the proof: "For if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory." By "rulers" he means Pilate, Herod and their circle, and by "the Lord of glory" God made flesh.

This quotation is not found in the Old Testament in these exact words, but in other words with the same meaning. Isaiah says, "Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" and "Who will tell of his generation?" And Moses says, "The hidden things belong to the Lord our God." What God keeps hidden, then, clearly escaped both eye and heart.

We must not suppose, however, that God arbitrarily revealed the mystery to some and left others to perish in ignorance. We must know and be convinced that, by his power of foreknowledge, he measured out to each what was deserved and beneficial, for he foresees each person's choice even before that person comes into being.
By "the depths of God" he means his deepest dispensations, which are hidden from us.

By these words he shows that the Spirit searches, not as one who is ignorant but as one who knows. Since some say that "Spirit" here means the Father and others the Son, we must answer both. It cannot mean the Father, for he says, "We have received not the spirit of the world but the Spirit that is from God," yet no one is "from" him [?]. If it were said of God, from whom would God be? One might suspect it means the Son, but he cannot be the one the passage is about. Who would say that God the Word searches in order to learn the things of God? And if they claim that the Son is taught, how did they fail to see from what follows that, just as a man's spirit knows what is in him, so does the Spirit of God? Besides, the whole passage plainly points to the Holy Spirit. We should note that he says the Holy Spirit is "from God," but he did not say the unclean spirit is "from the world," only "of the world." The Paraclete is not a part of God, whereas the devil, having come into being, is a part of creation. The Holy Spirit, however, is from God.

It is not to show that, just as in us our spirit is superior to us, so in God the Spirit is superior to him, that he immediately said, "For who among men knows the things of a man except the spirit that is in him?" But what of the Spirit's being "from God" [?]? What is "in him" is a part completing the whole human being, whereas "from him" indicates the cause. We should note that God and the Holy Spirit are two persons, whereas a man and the spirit in him are not two persons but one man. So, to show that the Father and the Spirit are exactly the same in knowledge, he compared the knowledge of the spirit in us with the knowledge of the Father and the Spirit. Just as in us, in one and the same spirit, that is, the soul and the mind, there is no discord of union [?], but we know what we know, so also in the Father and the Holy Spirit there is no discord of knowledge, but identity. "So that we may know the things freely given to us by God": the Spirit has given them, and the mind has grasped them.

"Which we also speak." Again he points out something further. Not only, he says, do we not discover by reasoning what has been revealed to us, but we also preach it, not dressing it up with words but "comparing spiritual things with spiritual": by the power of the Spirit we both understand his revelations and preach them in due order. "Comparing spiritual things with spiritual": when a second revelation interprets and clarifies an earlier one, those who receive the revelations compare the second with the first, and finding them the same, they gain greater assurance of the revealed truth.

God and the Holy Spirit are two persons, whereas a man and the spirit in him are not two persons but one man. But what he means is this: just as in a human being there is no discord of knowledge, so also the Father and the Spirit have one knowledge, so that in this respect the Spirit would not search as one who is ignorant. Again, in the case of the man he said "the spirit that is in him," but in the case of the Holy Spirit he did not say "that is in God" but "that is from God." There is a great difference between "in him" and "from God": what is "in him" completes the whole human being, while "from him" indicates the cause.

He spoke precisely when he called the Holy Spirit "from God," as a living and subsistent being, and the unclean spirit "of the world," as something that completes its substance; for the devil, having come into being, is part of his creation. In any case, we do not seek by reasoning to embellish what has been revealed to us. Rather, we compare spiritual things with spiritual, whenever a second revelation interprets and clarifies the first teaching, vision or miracle. The later things are compared with the earlier and found to be the same, and from this agreement we receive the fullest assurance of the truth. "Comparing" can also mean the opposite, namely "distinguishing and separating"; but the first sense is better.

"But the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit." By "natural" he means the person who follows his own reasonings. "For they are foolishness to him." So deep is spiritual revelation that it seems foolishness to the wise of this world; so far is God's revelation beyond their grasp.
For the grace of the Holy Spirit, displaying its power, refuted the skilled reasoner, not by skilful argument but by the force of its miracles.

Spiritual people do not overturn reasonings with reasonings. They have received the mind that comes from God and the revelation that comes from there, and they speak from these. So whoever opposes them is not refuting reasonings but setting himself against the knowledge of God. That is why he says: "For who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ," that is, his knowledge.

By "natural" he means the person who follows his own reasonings, or who is sick with the reasonings of the soul and not sound in the knowledge of the truth, just as he calls "fleshly" the person who is sick with fleshly desires and a slave to pleasures. So the natural man cannot be receptive to the truth; his soul is so corrupted that he regards God's dispensation and grace as foolishness. "And he cannot know them, because he is spiritually examined." The natural man, looking for clever reasonings about the cross, rejects the preaching as foolish and unconvincing. And since he pays no attention to the Spirit's miracles, he can no longer even understand that he is setting himself against the truth and is being refuted by the power and miracles of the Spirit. For "is examined" means "is thoroughly and searchingly refuted." But the spiritual man, who has received the Spirit, as the signs he displays show, refutes everything that others argue wrongly, while he himself is refuted by no one. Then, to confirm his words, he cites passages from the Old Testament and says:

"Will instruct" means "will correct." We have the mind of Christ our God. If human beings cannot attain to knowing the mind of God, then neither can they know ours, since we have the mind and wisdom of God.

Unbelievers are more readily won over by miracles. That is why I gave you a word, but not the perfect, hidden wisdom, the dispensation concerning the Passion, which only the perfect who believe accept. Further, he figuratively calls moral teaching and believing through signs "milk," and the proclamation of divine doctrines "solid food." "Milk" can also mean the easy commandments: honour your father and mother, you shall not commit adultery, and the like, and "Come, follow me." Then, when he says, "You are fleshly and walk in a merely human way," he means this: you honour what belongs to men and do not seek the things of God.
In place of "equal in ministry."
Some of what he says is drawn from farming, some from building. He says that he himself planted, made the beginning, and laid God's foundation.
He urges those who build on the foundation after him not to do the building carelessly. By "foundation" he means the faith and the preaching.

Christ is not called the foundation of creation, as the Arians falsely insist, but of faith. Christ was preached, and the whole building rises on this foundation. Those who teach preach one faith and proclaim the gospel way of life, but it is up to us to make ourselves precious stones, or wood, or grass, or straw. So when he says, "Let each one take care how he builds on it," it is not about the way of life. About what, then? "For no one can lay any foundation other than the one that is laid." The teacher proclaims Christ and passes on his commandments. What remains is to become like gold through purity or like grass through weakness. So when he urges, "Let each one take care," and so on, he is addressing those who want to be named after the people who baptize or teach. "If anyone's work that he has built on it survives": you see that the builder builds well, but sometimes the work does not survive because a person's choice changes for the worse. "If anyone's work is burned up, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet only as through fire." The word order is inverted, and it should be read like this: "If anyone's work is burned up, he will suffer loss, yet only as through fire." In other words, the work will be burned up and he will suffer loss in this way, as through fire, "but he himself will be saved," since the turn for the worse did not happen through his fault.

This is said by hyperbaton, so that it runs like this: "If anyone's work remains, he will receive a reward, and he himself will be saved. If anyone's work is burned up, he will suffer loss and will be burned as through fire." For how will he himself be saved if the work he built is burned up? Rather, it is so: he is judged as through fire, to see whether he left out anything that served to correct sinners or to admonish them, as in Ezekiel.

Again he turns to those who are confident in their own wisdom. What follows will make clear that he calls believers temples of God, while those confident in words are the ones he says destroy the temple of God: "If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool." Why, then, does someone confident in outside wisdom destroy the temple? If you are God's temple, you ought to have him as the one who teaches you and reveals things to you. But if you leave aside the one who dwells within and rely on your own understanding, you no longer make the temple a temple; you destroy it. "If anyone among you thinks that he is wise": this is aimed at those who were struck and harmed by outside learning, for he drew a distinction by saying "among you."

Those who have been instructed, who have received the word of knowledge within themselves and have not been shaken from the teaching, he calls temples of the Holy Spirit and unshakable dwellings of the Spirit who has come to dwell in them. Those who have done something worthy of the Spirit's working he calls spiritual, just as we call people rhetoricians or craftsmen once they have shown their skill in rhetoric or in their craft. So those who take on another teaching drawn from outside wisdom have destroyed their own reasoning, the temple of the Spirit, by counterfeiting the faith. For this reason he threatens that they will be destroyed by God: having abandoned the teacher who dwells within them, they went astray after outside wisdom, which is well suited to supply the means of deceit.
With these words he forbids the wisdom of this world, since it readily leads to deceit, and he has singled out those who are struck by his reproof.

Having charged them not to accept outside wisdom, he teaches them not to boast in wise men either. Such boasting is paltry when all things are yours. The apostles are yours, for they were sent for the sake of those who would benefit. The world is yours, since it came into being for you to enjoy. Life is yours, as people who are being saved. Death is yours too, for if death held no terrors, the life to come would not have been preferred. The things present and the things to come are mentioned on the same principle: those who despise present things as fleeting obtain the things to come. So all the things named are yours, because you too have become Christ's, and those who have been joined to Christ are pleasing to God.
All things are under you. How, and in what way? Because you too have become Christ's. And to show that those who have been joined to Christ are pleasing to God, he added: "and Christ is God's."
It is enough for us to be honored as servants of Christ. For some to be named after us is offensive.

You regard us as servants of God, but which servant is faithful is not for you to inquire, for that is where the danger lies among you. Nor is it fitting for teachers to be judged by their disciples. Why does he say this? Because he saw that some of the teachers who were unworthy were being honored by them, while those who were worthy were overlooked, and from this he foresaw that there would be divisions among them. That is why he reproaches them all the more sharply, hastening to check this passion.

So that he would not seem to be speaking arrogantly because he had been slighted, he all but says: Do not suppose that I am sending you these words for my own sake. I do not conduct myself so as to be examined by you; I consider that beneath me, with regard to you and to every human being. He calls a human being "a human day," pointing to the fleeting and short-lived character of human life. Then, since it seems a great thing to say, "I am conscious of nothing against myself," he added, "but I am not justified by this." For it is possible to stumble through ignorance and not be stung by one's conscience. Moreover, it is not refraining from evil that justifies; it is the achievement of virtue that makes one perfect. He probably said this out of modesty as well. So do not think more highly than befits you, but wait for the judge.

Throughout he keeps to his purpose, bringing to their senses those who wish to be named after one person and not after another, for this is what people do when they judge who is worthy and who is not. So do not think more highly than befits you, but wait for the judge. A put-on character can deceive you, but nothing hidden could escape the one who brings to light the things hidden in darkness. He said this because much was happening among them through deceit, and unworthy men were being honored.

Those who were honored were by no means all good; they possessed virtue only as far as outward appearance, while those who were truly good were overlooked. Otherwise he would not have said these things.

He puts forward himself and Apollos, and says nothing about the persons of those who demanded to be honored and to have the disciples named after them, so that, as he says, "you may take from us a pattern and an example" of behaving with moderation toward your teachers. "Do not think beyond what is written concerning us, but regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God, and do not dishonor some of the teachers while honoring others."
In these words he exposed their attitude more plainly. The man who was named after one person and overlooked another was puffed up on behalf of the one and directed his arrogance against the other.

You who want to be called after this man, or to abandon that one, who distinguishes you? Do you not wait for the judge? You who are a hearer wait for the judge, and yet you subject your teacher to your own judgment?

You, a layman: who judges you for what you think or do, that you dare to judge others, and teachers at that? Is it not the Lord? If, then, you the disciple wait for the Lord as judge, how can you subject your teacher to your own judgment, calling one worthy and another unworthy?
Why do you think you have an advantage that you neither have nor have received? He means surpassing understanding, by which one might be able to judge and test teachers.
Even if you have received understanding from God, you must give glory to God who gave it, and not think highly of yourself and be exalted, as though you were displaying an advantage of your own.

Not that their condition was really like this; he shows rather that this was how they were disposed, holding false opinions about themselves and thinking they were filled with all knowledge, to the point of even judging their teachers. "Already" the gifts have become cloying to you and are no longer always longed for. "Without us" means: while we have not yet reigned, you have reigned ahead of us. By putting "would that you did" in the middle, he shows his own feeling toward them. Then by saying "so that we too might reign with you," he makes it plain that he counts their achievements as his own goods. It is also not unreasonable to read "you have reigned" and "you have become rich" as questions, so that the words match the tone of "you are already filled."
For as I see it, if you have become rich and have reigned without us, then we who have endured everything have become last, men condemned to death.
To men, he says, because they see our sufferings; and to angels, because they marvel at our steadfastness.

These words are of the same kind. Those who teach you live in contempt and lowliness, so that they are even thought fools by the world, while you who are taught want to be already in wealth and honors in Christ. He says this to show that in spiritual gifts the disciple is not above the teacher.

We endure all things for Christ's sake and humble ourselves to this very day. How then can you, living in the flesh, be preferred by God to those who toil, who are persecuted, who are reviled, who are beaten? Through all of this he teaches how a Christian ought to be and to humble himself.

That is, "scrapings." We have become like sweepings and dung taken out of a house that is being cleaned, despised by everyone; and we are the refuse of all, subjecting ourselves to all people for Christ's sake. "Offscouring" is the word for the cloth that wipes away the sweat of someone who is laboring and wipes off the distress that lies upon him.

Having censured them strongly in what came before, he now comforts them, so that by mixing what is astringent with what is sweet he may blend a medicine with saving power. "To shame you" means to put you to confusion.

By calling himself a father, and those after whom they were named tutors, he shows that his affection for them is more genuine than that of the others, and that since they are being admonished by a father they ought not to be indignant.
Become imitators of me in not looking down on anyone and not exalting yourselves, and in being called not after anyone else but after Christ.

You see that the things he said, "we are weak, but you are strong," and all the rest, were said because some were puffed up and exalted. "But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of those who are puffed up but their power." With these words he rebukes them strongly, and by threatening to come in person he himself bears witness that they are capable of correction. He announces his coming as though they would turn out to be humbled, correcting them by his words before he arrives. Yet he added "if the Lord wills." Indignation drove him to say "I will come," but reverence reminded him to add that finest of additions, "if the Lord wills." And here he lays bare what he had earlier said in a veiled way, so as not to seem to rebuke them too harshly: "for the kingdom of God is not in word," meaning, clearly, cultivated eloquence. For the apostles did not teach and preach without words.
From these words too it is clear that "we are weak, but you are strong" and the rest were said because some were puffed up.
He announces his coming so that they may correct themselves before he arrives. Indignation compelled him to say "I will come," but out of reverence he added "if the Lord wills."

From these words too it has become clearer that he is indignant with those who boast in the wisdom of this world, for he does not wish to disparage ordinary speech. Indeed, this is what he too used in preaching to them, as to everyone.

Since correction is of two kinds, sometimes by admonition for the compliant and sometimes by force and compulsion for the stiff-necked, he has kindly left the choice between them to the Corinthians, so that they may repent and correct themselves. By "rod" he means the coercive power of the Spirit, which Paul used against Elymas, and which God used against Paul himself.

They were puffed up not because that man had a woman in the way described, but because he was an eminent speaker. They did not mourn that he had his father's wife; they were puffed up that he was well educated. For their mourning would either have cut off the fornicator if he persisted, or would have driven out the outrage of the deed and brought him back.

Not simply "done" but "perpetrated": he did not fall by being carried away, but actually committed the evil in deed. He says he is present in spirit, casting his vote with them and joining in the condemnation (by "spirit" he means the gift), when they are assembled together with the power of Christ. Those puffed up over the fornicator because of his eloquence were only part of the whole, but he calls on everyone to assemble to condemn the fornication.

So that he would not seem to be stirred without reason, he gives the cause of his anger as well: not only is there fornication reported among you, but fornication of a kind not found even among the Gentiles. And you think highly of yourselves because you have been adorned with the wisdom of this world. You should have mourned over him, because he has dared a fornication that is not customary even among the others. Such mourning would either have cut off the fornicator if he persisted in his fornication, or would have cut off the outrage itself and brought the man back, so that his spirit might be saved.

He did not say "done" but "perpetrated," to make plain even by this that he committed the evil with long persistence, and did not sin by being carried away in a way that would give him some excuse. The apostle was capable of condemning him on his own, but he wants the Corinthians to cast their votes with him, so that in this way they might be set right by being separated from fellowship with the lawbreaker, especially those who were puffed up over education. He does this not by placing him under Satan's authority, for by doing that he would have pleased Satan. Rather, since we are accustomed to attribute to Satan all the hardships of life, such as illnesses, griefs, bereavements and other troubles, as the apostle himself says somewhere, "A thorn was given me, a Satan, to buffet me," in the same way he now orders him to be handed over to Satan, that is, to the hardships of life.
They said that "the spirit" means not the soul but the gift.

He hands him over to the afflictions of life; this is what "for the destruction of the flesh" means, not for the ruin of the soul, so that, roused by what happens to his body, he may repent and the spirit in him, that is, the gift, may be saved. For he does not mean the soul here, as though the flesh would not rise and the soul alone would be saved.
You see that they were boasting over that man, paying no attention to the outrageousness of his offense, but puffed up by his eloquence.
For they were boasting over him, paying no attention to his offense but puffed up by his education.
He orders him to be expelled, so that the others who associate with him may not also rush shamelessly into sin.
He calls sin the old leaven, with which the old man was leavened.
He carries the type over to the reality. The unleavened bread of the Jews, not mixed with old leaven, foreshadowed the new people, not mixed with the sins of the old man.

The lamb sacrificed among the Jews signified the passion and the [?] mystery of the dispensation of the cross. He says what follows because leaven is in some way more elaborate, and unleavened bread simpler.
He kept to the figure, as if to say: not in a wicked and evil life, but in a life that has no admixture of that old leaven; for that is what "with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth" means.

He wrote it not in another letter but in this one. He does not forbid association with outsiders because, if they shunned everyone of that kind, the preaching would be hindered; nearly everyone among the Gentiles was like that, so to speak, and these were the very people who stood to benefit from associating with believers. He shows, then, that one should rebuke one's own people when they sin, but appeal to those who have gone astray.
"I wrote" refers not to another letter but to this one, for he says, "But now I have written to you." And "Remove the wicked man from among yourselves" is a saying of Moses which Paul repeats.

He recalls a saying found in the Old Testament to show not only that they themselves benefit, as people rid of a plague, but also that such a thing is no innovation: the lawgiver too judged that such people should be cut off.
He was right to say this, for a person becomes judge of his own household, not of outsiders. But God is judge of all, since he is master of all.
He reproaches them because, though there were saints able to judge their cases, they were being judged by unbelievers.

Having said above, "You judge those inside, but God will judge those outside," he now subjects the whole world to the judgment of the saints. Here, they examine the lives of believers in order to correct them; there, they are entrusted with judging the world, not to correct the ways of those who have sinned but to convict and condemn them. So the twelve apostles will judge the twelve tribes, as Jews judging Jews, on the grounds that they believed the prophets themselves, and yet [?] disbelieved and for that reason rejected Christ. The other holy ones, that is, those from the Gentiles, will condemn those who did not turn away from idols and believe in the true God. So there is no disagreement between the evangelist and the apostle, for Christ was speaking in both. For it is written: "The queen of the south will rise up and condemn this generation," and "The men of Nineveh will rise up and condemn you."

Did he not say, "and if the world is judged by you"? Here, however, by "angels" he does not mean those who are angels by nature, but the ministering priests, the teachers of the people, whom the saints may well judge for having taught falsely about Christ. By saying, "How much more the things of this life?" he showed that he was speaking not of those who are angels by nature, but of those who hold an angelic rank and carry out spiritual duties. And if he meant angels in the proper sense, he clearly meant those who rebelled and fell away from God. Priests, at any rate, have been called angels, as Malachi says: "The lips of a priest will guard knowledge, and they will seek the law from his mouth, for he is an angel of the Lord of hosts." So it is these priests who led the people astray whom we judge, and likewise those who founded heresies and perverted the teaching of Christ.
The least member of the church is preferable to an unbeliever. Still, the apostle seems to have left unsaid what is obvious, that the more serious charges must be reserved for those who are perfect.
You show yourselves defeated by the devil not only by going to law before unbelievers, but by the very fact of having lawsuits with one another.
He spoke of the one working of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit in the righteous, teaching the oneness of their essence.

In "by anything" he is speaking not of a person but of a thing, for the discussion concerns these: "Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food, but God will do away with both the one and the other."

In "by anything" he is speaking not of a person but of a shameful thing and a passion. By speaking about himself he urges the others to self-control. Knowing that the belly was the cause of their greed, since most people will dare anything for the pleasures of the belly, he teaches that it is unprofitable to be a slave to the stomach.

We know that food is for the stomach. The stomach too has been set apart for food, but these are temporary, and God will put an end to them, for after the resurrection, when immortality is given, there will be no more need for food. Why then are you so eager for temporary things, which give rise to fornication and shameful pleasures?

It is clear that food and eating are temporary. The body, however, has been set apart not for fornication but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. And the body is not temporary; it will be raised to everlasting life after the pattern of Christ.
By the body and members of Christ he means the body of those who have believed and been baptized.

Whatever sin someone commits in feeding or clothing the body, he does it to adorn the body and supply its needs, and so for the body's honor. But the man who joins himself to a prostitute, making his own body one body with her, outrages and dishonors it.

Clothing and adornment are outside the body, so the man who sins in these matters sins outside the body. Or again: the man who reviles or lies harms and robs others, and one who commits adultery does so with another man's wife, but the fornicator outrages himself, since the harm from the deed does not pass over to anyone else. So whatever sin a person commits, he has sinned, but not against his own body, nor has he dishonored his own flesh as the fornicator has.

Yet the murderer, staining his hand with blood, also sins against his own body, and so does the reviler, who bloodies his tongue, as it were, with abuse. But the fornicator, he says, plunges his whole self into the mire of fornication. So Paul went along with the common opinion in saying that the other sins are outside the body. Others say that the passage means this: the fornicator sins against his own body, that is, against the very constitution of his own body, against, one might say, the very makeup of a human being and the origins of our birth. It is as if he were saying: stop outraging, by unlawful intercourse, the workshop of nature from which your own body sprang. Still others say that Paul is eager to show that the sin of fornication is beyond pardon. Having said above, "Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?" and so on, and having shown from this that the fornicator offends against the members of Christ, he then adds, "Every sin," and so on. For the reviler, the robber or the greedy man has offended against the person he reviled or wronged, but the fornicator sins against his own body, which is the members of Christ. Since through the adoption of the Spirit he belongs to the body of Christ, he will be charged not only with fornication but with impiety too, for making the members of Christ members of a prostitute and outraging his own body as the temple of Christ. That is why he goes on: "Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God?" and so on. For by the sin of fornication you sin against the body as against God's temple, and it drives the Holy Spirit away. This is not because the rest of the sins go unpunished, for all of them bring loss of the kingdom, but because, given the matter at hand, he was eager to declare fornication more grievous than all the others. He wanted to tear the passion out by the roots, since among the Corinthians it was being committed in a particularly impious way: "It is actually reported," he says, "that there is fornication among you," and so on.

The fornicator is guilty of impiety as well, for by outraging his own body he has defiled the temple of the Holy Spirit. He says this because some were committing fornication with contempt, considering it a small fault or no fault at all, since Moses did not even mention it in his Decalogue. The "price" is the saving blood of Christ, which he gave as a ransom for us. So glorify God not only in the gift but also in the body, so that nature, free will and the gift may all glorify God.

"So glorify God in your body and in your spirit." Not only in the gift but also in the body, so that nature, free will and grace may glorify the benefactor in harmony. Others have taken "the spirit" to mean the soul.

He wrote this in reply to the clergy, for it was they who had written to the apostle. He forbade fornication as unlawful; he permitted the union of marriage as godly and as a safeguard against fornication; and he praised continence as the more perfect way.

He teaches that those joined in marriage have authority over each other rather than over themselves. It is a fine debt for those who live together when, in addition to their harmony in other things, they know to render this to each other as something owed. The apostle used such great condescension by way of accommodation in order to cut out fornication, the worst of diseases, teaching that those joined in marriage have authority over each other rather than over themselves.

Since he has said that they are each other's slaves, he goes on to say that they must not deprive each other of themselves, except by a pious agreement. In this way they will not become causes of fornication to each other, nor destroy their authority over each other by separating against each other's will.

Making allowance for the nature of the body, I say that you must come together again. I do not say this in order to shut you out from continence altogether, for I wish everyone to live in continence, as I do myself.

He advises widows, and unmarried men who have not practiced virginity, to live in continence, but to marry if they are overcome by the flesh. In this he shows that continence is a great thing. Still, he permits marriage as a good bond.

He would not have said “a wife should not separate from her husband” about those who separate in order to renounce the world and devote themselves to Christ. “Let her either be reconciled to her husband or remain unmarried” is evidently said about those who part because of some quarrel.

Above he spoke of separation for the sake of continence; here he speaks of separation that comes about through squabbling. Then he said, “not I but the Lord.” For there are some things the apostle says on his own account, and the Lord did not say everything himself. He means: I am now charging you with what the Lord charged in the Gospels concerning the married, when he said, “What God has joined together, let no one separate.” And the words “but if she does separate, let her remain unmarried” also agree with what the Lord said: “If anyone marries a divorced woman, he commits adultery, and so does she if she is married to another.”

When he says “I, not the Lord,” he is not laying down a law against the Lord. He means that some things the Lord said himself, while some things are now said for the first time by the apostle, about separation from an unbeliever. And he teaches that unbelief does not prevail over faith; rather, the faith of the partner sanctifies even the unbeliever.
He is speaking not of taking an unbeliever in marriage, but of bearing with an unbeliever.
The children are holy, that is, clean and not defiled even by unbelief, for in them the faith of the parents prevails over the unbelief.

To one God has assigned the task of saving, to the other that of being saved, giving each what each deserves. The words “as God has assigned to each” refer not to having an unbeliever but to bearing with an unbeliever.

Circumcision is not good in itself, but because it is God's commandment; and uncircumcision is God's workmanship, not a reward for the uncircumcised. Then he speaks about the slave: do not be eager for a temporary freedom, but even if you can gain it, rather make use of your slavery. For the reward is greater when someone who is occupied in serving people does not neglect to please God. Let each remain in the state in which he was called: the slave without resenting his slavery, and the free man without being proud, for with God there is no difference.

In this respect the believing slave has nothing less than the free man, for with God even a slave is regarded as free, and he has been set free by God. This is what “is the Lord's freedman” shows: he has been set free by the Lord himself. And the one who was free when he was called to the faith will have nothing more than the slave; like the slave, he is a slave of Christ.

Grace knows no difference between slavery and mastery. So do not flee from slavery as though it were unworthy of the faith, for because of it you have nothing less than anyone else in the faith. And even if it should be possible for you to gain your freedom, your concern should rather be how you may use it better for what is needful, as one who has taken care to be free from evil. And to show that the free man has nothing more with Christ on this account, and that the slave is not lessened on this account either, he adds: “For whoever was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord's freedman; likewise whoever was called as a free man is Christ's slave.”
That is: do not, for the sake of your needs, live in a servile and unfree way, serving people while abandoning the true Master, by whose blood you were bought.

How is it that elsewhere he says, “If you seek proof of Christ speaking in me,” but now says, “I have no command of the Lord”? Who would accept what he says if he is saying things the Lord did not command him? But clearly he does not mean that he has no command to teach about virginity. He means that he had not received authority from God to command you to remain virgins, but rather to give his opinion and to advise that virginity is good and profitable. That is why, as one giving advice, he says “I think” and calls it “good,” and leaves it to his hearers to choose it or not. The thing is pleasing to God, as the Lord said that some have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom, calling virginity being a eunuch because of its inactivity. So he says he has no command, but he left it to free judgment, saying, “Let the one who is able to receive this receive it.” Then, by calling himself trustworthy, he shows that what he says is trustworthy and worthy of being a command. And when he says “I think,” it is not that he doubts that virginity is good; he is guarding against its being taken for a command.
He showed that he introduces virginity not as an accusation against marriage; he recommends virginity in order to spare the saints, since marriage fills the flesh with birth pangs and toils.

He showed that he introduces virginity not as an accusation against marriage, but out of concern for freedom from the affairs of this life. Then, saying “but I would spare you,” he recommends virginity in order to spare the saints, not as an accusation against marriage.

He gives another reason why he prefers virginity, showing everywhere that in preferring holiness he [does not?] accuse marriage: the world is near its end, and we must recognize that what we have we do not really have, for we leave it behind, “so that those who have may be as though they had not.” If it is good for those who have to have as though they did not have, how much more is it good for the virgin not even to enter into marriage? “And those who use this world as though not using it to the full”: by this he casts out immoderate enjoyment, but leaves room for what is needed. For “the form of this world is passing away” shows that it is not the world that passes away; rather, the form of the present life is changed, corruption into incorruption. Cities, walls, laws, farming, crafts: these are laid upon this life like a kind of shape, and that shape undergoes change.

By this he shows how short human life is, so that people may turn to repentance, despising temporary things as those who have already reached the end of life. And if it is good for those who have to have as though they did not have, how is virginity not better?
That is: let neither the painful things of this life cast you down, nor the things that seem to deserve joy make you overjoyed, for everything here is temporary and does not last.

Systems of government, laws, farming, crafts and trade are like a form and shape of the world. There will be no need for them once corruption has been changed into incorruption. So he shows that it is not the world that passes away, but the present form of the world.
He has shown why he said, “but I would spare you”: so that you may not waste your cares on things that do not last. What follows shows this even more clearly.

He has given the reason why virginity is preferable to marriage. It is not because of the marriage bed or abstaining from it, but because marriage is full of cares, whereas a life lived for God occupies the mind with piety [?].

I want you to be free from anxiety, so that you may not waste your cares on things that do not last, distracted by the needs of this life. That is why virginity is preferable to marriage: not because of abstaining from the marriage bed, but because marriage draws the mind away from piety.

Some think he is speaking of a man behaving improperly with regard to himself, meaning “if anyone thinks he is behaving improperly with regard to his own virginity.” But it is not so, and what follows shows this. For he says, “So then he who gives her in marriage does well, and he who does not give her in marriage does better.” But no one gives himself in marriage; one is given by someone else.
Better than this blessed state is to remain as she is, for the one brings bodily rest, the other a more perfect piety.
This is said by way of comparison. She is blessed if she marries and has a husband's protection, but more blessed if, looking to piety, she does not marry but devotes herself to God.

The Corinthians were eating food sacrificed to idols, saying, “For us there is no such thing as idol-sacrifice, for I sanctify the food by calling on the name of Christ, and I eat.” So he shows that they are not the only ones wise enough to know this, and says: “We know that we all have knowledge.” In other words: what you know, I know too; but what is happening to you is not happening to me.

There is no need to examine what you know and I know too. But what I know, that one must not eat for the sake of the weak, you do not know, though I do. Why then are you puffed up by a knowledge that does not amount to as much as my knowledge? So he adds: “If anyone among you thinks he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know.” For instance, what I know, you do not yet know. “But if anyone loves God, he is known by him.” Whatever we, as human beings, suppose we know, we do not yet know anything. What, then, is blessedness? To love God and to be known by him. This is not because he does not know those who do not love him, but because he makes those who love him his own. For “knowing” is also used in the sense of making one's own, just as “not knowing” is used in the sense of estrangement, as in the Lord's saying, “Depart from me; I never knew you.”
