The Corinthians were saying, “An idol is nothing; so we take no account of sacrificial meats, since we eat them in the name of Christ, and we are not harmed [?].” He shows that they are not the only ones wise enough to know this, but others know it too: that there is no such thing as sacrificial meat. So: what you know, I know too; but what is happening to you is not happening to me. Such knowledge, then, puffs up and does harm, if you know your own point but not the other one too, that love builds up. For out of love for your weak brother you must not eat in an idol's temple, so that he is not wounded.
The one among you who thinks he knows something knows nothing, for he did not recognize that others are harmed by these people's knowledge.

Even if we suppose we know something, we do not yet know anything. Blessedness is to love God and to be known by him, that is, to be made his own. For he is ignorant of no one, but he is said not to know the ungodly.

Having first said, “There is no God but one,” he added “the Father,” so as not to seem to exclude the Son from the Godhead. For in truth there is no other Father but one. In the same way, there is no other God the Son but one. And if the Father is no less Lord when the Son is called the one Lord, then clearly the Son is no less God when the Father is called the one God. “From whom are all things” does not indicate his substance, for created things do not come from the substance of God; rather, “from whom” indicates the will of the Father. Then, by saying “and we to him,” he lets us understand what is left out of the sentence: “but for us there is one God, and we hope in him.” Again something is left out of the words “and we through him”: “we have been called” or “we have been saved” is missing. He is not saying that we came into being through him, since by saying “all things” he already included us. Rather, “all things” refers to what came into being, and “we” to those who have been brought into his saving plan and are being saved.
What you gain is nothing, but the harm done to the weaker is great.
What knowledge? That God is one and that an idol is nothing in the world.

Whoever does not have this knowledge, that God is one and an idol is nothing in the world, is wounded, since he thinks he is eating idol-sacrifice. And your knowledge harms the one who is weak. For many even among those who have believed have not yet understood that there is no such thing as idol-sacrifice, and they are harmed by the believer who eats. What is gained by eating is not great, but the harm done to the weaker is serious.

I am not saying only that I will not eat idol-sacrifice; I will not even eat meat, if my brother is caused to stumble by it. For even in matters where he had a right, such as being maintained [?] by them, he would not allow himself to burden anyone. He establishes this with many arguments. First he recalls his own rank, to show the grounds on which he could reasonably have received support if he had wished, just as the others received from those who gave to them. “I too,” he says, “am an apostle and have authority of my own. I am not under anyone who compels me or prevents me from receiving. For even if the other apostles have something more than I do, in having been with Christ, I am not deprived of this either.”
To those who question whether I am an apostle, this is my defense: you yourselves, my seal, and the teaching you received.

Do I not give orders as an apostle? Do I not lay down laws for the churches? Am I under other teachers? I have the right, then, but I do not make full use of it, so that I may not cause anyone of little faith to stumble because of me.
The confirmation and the proof.
He shows that it has been laid down by law that those who serve either altars or the gospel should live from them.

By saying “woman” and adding “sister,” he indicated the propriety, modesty and purity of the woman who travelled with them, whether she was a wife or not. Clearly women did travel with Peter and the others, longing for their teaching. He does not say this to disparage them, far from it. He is showing the surpassing strictness of his own way of life, shaming the Corinthians into not living carelessly, so that they may not become a stumbling block to others.
Or are we alone forbidden to do the things that others also do? He included Barnabas as his fellow worker, so as not to seem proud, as though he alone were succeeding.
Am I speaking my own words? Does the law not say these things too?
“But I did not write this,” he says, “in order to get something from you. Far from it!”
It is nothing great if you abstain from idol-sacrifice for your brother's sake. For I too have made myself a slave to those to whom I am not subject, in order to benefit many.
By “Jews” he means those who belong by birth to the race of Israel; by “those under the law” he means those who are not of their race but follow the law of the Jews and have become proselytes.

By “those without the law” he means the Greeks, who are not under the law of Moses. He did not say, “To the Greeks I became as a Greek,” since he could not bear even to pretend to paganism. So by “those without the law” he means those who turned to the faith from the Gentiles.

To those from among the Greeks I seemed not to be under the law, and I put up with that reputation in order to rescue them from Jewish practices. So at the beginning he made concessions to everyone, going along with them, so that by accommodating himself to them a little he might draw them to himself. For people do not agree at all with those who agree with them in nothing, but they do agree with those who agree with them in part.
Since the gospel too seems not to make use of the law, I imitated its way of proceeding, ordering things as it intends, so that in this very respect I might share in it.
Since it seems right to follow the law of the gospel, I imitated its way of proceeding; for what it said, that I put into practice.

He does not mean that only one out of all of us is chosen; otherwise people would have despaired of themselves, looking at how hard success is. Clearly the image is taken with reference to the peoples he mentioned. All, he says, compete in this life as in a stadium, the Jews according to the law, the Greeks according to their error. But there is one word of truth, and it is this that wins and takes the prize. So run, that you may not be left behind with the others.

“What great thing is it,” he says, “if you exercise self-control in the flesh for your brother's sake?” The competitor must exercise self-control in everything: in anger, in love of glory, and in all else. They do it to receive a perishable crown, but we an imperishable one.
He did not say this without reason. He was correcting those who, for the sake of their bellies, pretend to philosophize that idol-sacrifice is not idol-sacrifice.
He did not say this without reason. He was correcting those who, for the sake of their bellies, pretend to eat sacrificial meats indifferently, in faith.

The inspired Paul brings forward the types from the Old Testament and the shadows there that prefigured the truth to come, in order to bring the Corinthians to their senses by comparing them with the people of old. For if, he says, those who were baptized into Moses, who was a type of Christ, in the cloud and in the sea, and who ate the manna, the spiritual food, and drank the spiritual drink from the rock, were struck down in the wilderness when they turned to drunkenness, fornication and idolatry, because they insulted the type and the shadow, what would those not suffer who sin against the truth itself?

They were saying, “For me there is no idol, for I give thanks and eat.” This, he says, is putting the Lord to the test. For when you do what Jesus did not command, as though you were trusting him, you are testing him rather than believing.

He says this to those who say, “For me an idol is nothing, for I give thanks and eat,” which is putting him to the test. For when you do what the Lord did not command, as though you were trusting him, you are testing him rather than believing.

The coming of Christ, he says, has reached you, and after it there will no longer be commandment, law or prophets. For by “the ends” he does not mean the last generation, in which the world will be brought to its consummation, but the final way of life, the life in Christ, at which the consummation of the ages will arrive.
He did not pray that they would not be tempted, since a man who has not been tempted is untested; he prayed that they would be tempted in such a way as to be able to bear it.

From this he shows that those among them who had believed endured some unpleasant treatment from their fellow citizens. Then he did not pray that they would not be tempted, since a man who has not been tempted is untested, but that they would be tempted in such a way as to be able to bear it.
You see that everything he said before was building up to this.
He has arrived at what he was building up to. For everything he said before was said and built up in order to draw them away from idolatry.
Do not look at their idols, which are nothing, but at the intention with which they sacrifice to demons and not to God. For what is done there amounts to a denial of God.

It is written that God said to them through Moses, “They made me jealous with what is no god; they provoked me with their idols.” Since the Corinthians were eating idol-sacrifice, he says, “Or are we provoking the Lord to jealousy?”, that is, are we provoking him to anger? “Are we stronger than he?” By this he showed that the Lord does not want us to eat idol-sacrifice. So, he says, do not want what the Lord does not want, as though you were stronger and wiser than he.

Or are we stirring him to jealousy and provoking him? For Moses says, “They made me jealous with what is no god; they provoked me with their idols.” He says this because the Corinthians were eating idol-sacrifice.

It was likely that, being scrupulous, they would no longer dare even to buy food, for fear of hearing, “You have bought idol-sacrifice.” So he calms their fear. By “conscience” he means not that of the one who knows that an idol is nothing, but that of someone who has seen the person buying idol-sacrifice and thinks that idol-sacrifice is something.
What you eat belongs to the Lord, since the earth belongs to him, and everything that fills it.
Do everything with caution, so that because of you people may glorify God and not stumble.

Do not become a cause of stumbling to Jews and Greeks: see that they do not shun the faith on the pretext of your bad conduct. Nor to the church of God: see that those of little faith are not caused to stumble.
He now praises them, although they had gone astray, so that from now on they might at least be persuaded by what he says.

He says this to encourage them rather than to approve of them, so that he may then make his exhortation take firm hold among them: “But I want you to know that the head of every man is Christ, the head of the woman is the man, and the head of Christ is God.”

If someone takes this impiously, he takes it as referring to the Godhead; if piously, as referring to the incarnation. For the subject now is not coming into being; after all, the man did not make the woman. Nor does the order Paul used have this in view, but only subordination, and not subordination through difference of nature. Indeed, it is not the Godhead of the Only-begotten that is in view here at all, but the incarnation, which is closer in nature to the man and the woman.

The followers of Arius say: “Just as Christ is the head of man because he is his maker, so God is the head of Christ as his maker.” But they seem not to know what follows: “the head of the woman is the man.” The man is not her maker, and he is of the same substance as she is; and by the same reasoning we would be found to be of the same substance as Christ. So they talk nonsense on every point. Here “head” is used in the sense of ruling, not making. So whoever has Christ as ruler and head insults his own ruler if he sins. On this reasoning, by being subject to Christ we are subject to God the Father, since God is also the head of Christ.

By “prophesying” he means interpreting the prophets. Or else the difference between the prophets of old and the new ones lies in this: the old prophets prophesied in more general terms about the fall of the Jews, the calling of the Gentiles and Christ's coming in the flesh, while the new ones prophesied about particular matters, as Peter did in the case of Ananias.

From this it is clear that man is the image of God neither in his soul nor in his body. For if he were the image in either of these, the woman too would certainly have been called the image of God, since she too has the form of the body and has a soul just as the man does. But if the woman, who has the same soul and flesh as the man, is not called the image, then clearly man is the image of God in respect of rule. When the discussion concerns irrational creatures, the woman too is the image of God; but when man is compared with women, the man alone is the image. For male and female among human beings rule over everything on the earth, in the sea and in the air, but the man also rules over the woman, while no one on earth rules over the man. So just as no one among all beings rules over God, so no one among earthly beings rules over man. By “nature” we understand the truth of the things themselves.

The man is the image of God, not in body or soul, but in respect of rule. For along with everything else he also has the woman under his authority. And just as no one among all beings rules over God, so no one among earthly beings rules over man. And just as the man who properly obeys his Sovereign is the glory and praise of God, so the woman who is properly subject to the man is the man's glory.

The apostle says this because he had seen how harsh and hard to manage women are, and he reminds them that God has also set angels over us. Some say that the priests of the church are here called angels, and that women are to be veiled on their account, since women were not given the freedom to rule. But perhaps he said this because women also prophesied by the Holy Spirit. When the Spirit is at work, the ministering angels must be present, and for this reason the woman must be veiled.

He approved this on the basis of the custom of their own time, not ancient custom. Even those who wore their hair long in ancient times cut part of it off, [?] wearing it longer than was proper; but for a woman, cutting her hair was always considered improper.
By "factions" he means divisions over customs and practices, not over doctrines.

He reproaches them because, when they came together as if to share in the holy body, they did not wait for one another. Some were held up by their poverty and came late, and the wealthy, who arrived first, did not wait for them. Instead, out of gluttony, they neglected the Lord's supper and hurried to their own suppers. They held these lavishly in the church, as if to expose the want of those who had nothing, for while others went hungry they themselves got drunk. They got ahead of the communion and enjoyed their own delicacies.

Here by "spiritual gifts" he means the workings of the Holy Spirit, which the Spirit distributes to each according to his worth: to one the preaching of the gospel, to another prophecy, and to another something else. By saying "you were led away to idols" he shows the very great difference between prophecy and divination. Among the idols, those possessed by the unclean spirit are not in their right mind. They are carried off by the unclean spirit and do not act by their own free choice. That is what he means by "you were led away, being carried off." So he is saying: you know the working of the unclean spirit from what you suffered, but the things of the Holy Spirit work in purity. That is why the diviner's soul is darkened and he does not know what he is saying, while the prophet's soul becomes more full of light, learns what it did not know, and speaks what has been revealed to it. The demon, as an enemy, darkens the soul; the Spirit, as a benefactor, enlightens the soul when he comes to it. To show this he adds:

In every case, blasphemies against Christ are worked by the evil one, who clouds the soul. He says this to guard them against those who pretend to be inspired by God while speaking against Christ. Legion and the girl with the spirit of divination both named the Lord Jesus. So we do not say that whoever says this says it fully, for many are called "lords," even righteous men. What counts is to confess Christ's lordship and rule over all things. Perhaps those spirits also said this to tempt him, as the devil did when he led him up onto the mountain. That is why he does not accept their testimony, since it comes from the unworthy and from those who are tempting him.

The word of wisdom is the ability to understand what has been spoken in God's wisdom through the prophets and evangelists, and to set it before the hearers. The word of knowledge is the revelation of hidden things: someone who did not know them first learns them from grace and then speaks them. Faith is simply believing the preaching. Faith is not merely hearing it, but receiving faithfully what has been said. As for the discernment of spirits: divination imitated prophecy, in that it too seemed to foretell as the Holy Spirit does, so he gave the ability to tell these apart, so that people would not be led astray.

He compares Christ to a whole body made up of many members, meaning the church when he says "Christ." Christ is called the head of the church, and the church the body of Christ. He named the church "Christ," indicating the lesser by the greater.
He says this so that they will not look down on the humbler people in the church. Even if someone is lesser by nature, he still contributes to the common life of the church.
He did not say "members from members," but "many members from one member," for the head is a member of the whole body.
He did not say "from members," but "from a member," for the head is one member, and that is Christ, the head of the church.

Since he has spoken of members and a body, he begins with the most honored of the members after the head: the apostles. By "prophets" he means those in the church, not those under the law. Third come teachers. Do not be surprised that the teacher is placed before those who perform healings and miracles. Signs are given so that knowledge may be believed, and knowledge is presented through those who teach. "Helpers": elsewhere he puts it this way: "the one who leads, with diligence." "Administrators": those who govern the church.
Christ is the head of the church. After that member, he says, the apostles are the second members.
He does not mean those under the law, but those of the church.

With this he shows that they were proud of the gift of tongues, and of the other gifts as well. So he shows that love is the greatest. Those other gifts are given even to the unworthy, for the building up of the church, but the achievement of love belongs to the devout person. So he says: "Desire the greater gifts. And I will show you a way" that leads you to enjoy the greater gifts, and that way is love. Whoever loves fulfills the law, whoever fulfills the law is approved, and whoever is approved receives a spiritual gift.

He saw that they envied those who had the gifts but were not fervent in love, so he teaches that love is the highest good. Those gifts were sometimes given even to the unworthy for the building up of the church, but the achievement of love belongs to the devout person alone. So he calls love the way that leads us to the enjoyment of the greater gifts. For what is higher than the gift of love, which fulfills the whole law?

And what is the tongue of angels, who have no chest, no throat, no tongue, no voice? Moses says in Deuteronomy that God set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God. Clearly he set them at the time when he divided by languages those who tried to build the tower. Once they were no longer held in agreement by a common speech, and had in a sense become strangers to one another through their changed languages, angels were appointed so that each might guard the nation entrusted to him, and none might be wasted and perish. For this reason he calls the different languages "tongues of angels." We should understand that David speaks of the "bread of angels" without meaning that angels eat. In the same way Paul speaks of the "tongues of angels" without meaning that angels speak. In both cases the angels are meant as servants of God's ordinance. The tongue of men, then, is educated speech, for artful speech is acquired in addition to natural speech. The tongue of angels is natural language, divided into many languages.

"I have become a sounding brass or a clanging cymbal." This makes it clear that by "of angels" he means the variety and diversity of languages. Whoever speaks in other tongues among people who do not know them is like a cymbal: it produces only sound and conveys no meaning.

By the tongue of men he means rhetorical, grammatical, philosophical, intellectual, literary, technical and argumentative speech. But what tongue do angels have, who have no chest, no throat, no voice, nothing bodily at all? The "tongues of angels" are the different languages over which the angels were set at the dispersion after the building of the tower, so that each might guard the nation entrusted to him. We take the "bread of angels" to be the bread supplied at the angels' command. It does not mean that the angels ate it, but that they were ordered to provide it. In the same way, the "tongues of angels" are the different languages over which angels were set.

He called the different languages the sound of brass and the clanging of a cymbal. When someone does not know what is being said in another language, the speaker is to him like a cymbal making a meaningless noise and conveying no thought.

He calls a mystery anything that is unknown but revealed by the power of the Spirit. This is one mystery, as he says elsewhere: "For I do not want you to be ignorant of this mystery," and again: "Behold, I tell you a mystery."

A little later he teaches what love is, where he says, "Love is patient," and so on. So showing mercy is one thing and loving is another. Giving away one's possessions to the poor and handing oneself over to martyrdom, if they are not yet done for love's sake, slip without our noticing into vainglory and empty ambition. If we give, then, we must give out of love for the one who receives, or out of love for God who commanded it. And if we bear witness, we must endure it out of love for the Lord.
"Love never fails": that is, it never slips into sin.
What is partial is done away with when complete knowledge is given. We know only a few things, and far more remain hidden.

He is saying: when I was a child, I had a child's thoughts, but when I reached full manhood I gained understanding. I no longer simply knew that my father is my father, but also in what sense he is my father. In the same way, what I now know in part I will learn in the time of perfection. And what I now see dimly, as in a mirror, I will in due time know clearly. He did not say, "I will then know mysteries," which is what would have followed, but "I will be known." Whoever is known by God and made his own also comes to see the mysteries with his own eyes.

Since not all knowledge has yet been revealed to us, it remains for us to believe that all knowledge will be revealed. Those who believe do so in order to hope, and those who hope need love, so that we do not fall away from hope. That is why he said, "Greater than this is love," for through love the law is fulfilled.

Suppose he does not interpret, but only speaks in a tongue and does not make its meaning clear, because he does not have this gift of interpretation. He speaks mysteries, since it is evidently the Spirit who supplies the tongues, and he utters mysteries through the tongues. But he does not build up the church, which does not understand what he says. The one who speaks in a tongue builds himself up, knowing that he understood what he had not uttered before [?]. The grace of the Holy Spirit was in him, and he was being built up.
So if the one who speaks in tongues also interprets, he is not inferior to the prophet.

He says: strive for prophecy more than the other gifts. He said this because the gifts were given according to each person's way of life, and it was up to them to strive for and receive whatever they wished. When people speak in tongues, no one who hears them understands. Yet even if what is spoken is unclear to people, the one who speaks in the Spirit speaks mysteries, for the Spirit who supplies the tongues utters mysteries. But the one who prophesies benefits his hearers, because he speaks to them plainly.
The grace is greater if the one who speaks in tongues also receives the gift of interpretation. Perhaps he did not have both.
So if the one who speaks in tongues also interprets, he is not inferior to the prophet.

He is saying: How will I benefit you if I cannot speak to you about what God has revealed to me, or what I have come to know and grasp myself, or what I have understood from the prophets, or what I have decided to advise or teach you? If I speak about these things and you do not understand, how will I benefit you?
He is saying: consider that even with lifeless things like the flute and the lyre, if the notes are not distinct, what is played on the flute or the lyre becomes a confused jumble.
"Nothing is without sound": that is, no race of men.
By "spiritual things" he means the various gifts of the Holy Spirit.
He is saying: if I speak in some tongue that I do not know, without even knowing what it means, I am sure that my mind is unfruitful, since it does not grasp the meaning of what is said.

Let him pray to receive a double grace: both to speak in tongues and to interpret them. Praying in a tongue is the working of the Holy Spirit, but the mind remains unfruitful, because no one can understand what is said or benefit from it. So, he says, this is what I must do: make clear what the Spirit supplies to me, so that those who hear are built up, and so that my mind is not unfruitful for lack of grasping the meaning of the words.

Because no one can benefit from what is said or understand it, if I give thanks in a tongue the hearer does not answer you with the "Amen." By "the outsider" he means someone not yet baptized, like a man not enlisted in the army.
With a clear understanding and in the ordinary language.
Strive to become mature, so that you understand the Scriptures.

It should be noted that when the Jews are asked to show where God spoke to them in many tongues and they disobeyed, they cannot show it. But we can show that when the Holy Spirit came and was distributed in tongues, the Jews disbelieved and said, "They are full of new wine." So tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, while prophecy is not for unbelievers but for believers. Tongues build up when the hearer learns that the speaker is speaking a language he does not know. Even so, the hearer does not receive the benefit of spiritual teaching, because it does not get through to him when it is not understood. Prophecy concerns the future, and what is said about the future is believed not by just anyone but by the believer. The unbeliever needs someone who uses a language he does not know, and so shows that the Spirit of God is in him. So the tongue was a miracle in itself, while prophecy became a miracle when it was fulfilled, not when it was spoken. In divine Scripture unbelief is spoken of in two ways: the true unbelief of the pagans, and the little faith of the devout.
By "unbeliever" he means the pagan. By "outsider" he means someone not yet baptized, a man not enlisted in the army. At that time such people were not yet called catechumens or unbaptized.

He calls the writings of the other prophets "the law" too, since they lived according to the law. What Isaiah said was fulfilled when the Spirit came down upon the apostles: they spoke in tongues, and the Jews mocked them.

Tongues clearly do some good when the hearer realizes that the speaker is speaking a language he does not know and never learned from anyone. Even so, the hearer is not helped by it, because it is not understood. Prophecy is given to believers. It speaks about the future, and what it says is believed not by just anyone but by the believer. The sign is given to unbelievers so that they may believe what they see. Prophecy is given so that the hearer may accept what is said and bless the Lord. By "unbeliever" he means the pagan, and by "outsider" the catechumen. Sometimes, though, a person of little faith is also called an unbeliever.
Let each person build up the church with the grace he has received from God.

By saying "let him be silent" he taught that whoever speaks by the Holy Spirit speaks when he wishes and keeps silent when he wishes, as the prophets did. This is not true of those possessed by an unclean spirit, who speak even when they do not wish to, and speak things they do not know.

Here he shows that the Holy Spirit revealed the mysteries to people's souls, and those souls, once enlightened, revealed them to others. It is not as in divination, where the diviner does not know what he is saying. So he has now completed what he said at the start: "When you were pagans, you were led away to mute idols, being carried off." "Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said": the others are those who have the gift of discerning spirits. "If something is revealed to another who is sitting there, let the first be silent," since it is up to them to be silent at one time and to speak at another. "And the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets." He is saying: do not be afraid that by keeping silent you are rejecting the Spirit, for the gifts know how to yield to one another.
That is, those who have the gifts of discerning spirits.

Do not be afraid that by keeping silent you are rejecting the Spirit. The gifts know how to yield to one another, so that the church may be built up and there may be no confusion from everyone speaking at once.

He is saying: I am telling you nothing new, only what I preached. And it is not that I preached and you did not accept it; you also received it. Nor did you receive something vain and useless, but something by which you are being saved. He is about to say, "I made known to you how the Lord Jesus died for us," so he says "with what word," meaning this gospel, so that the resurrection might be believed. By dying for us, Jesus is the firstfruits of the resurrection. If death did not have to be destroyed, the Savior would not have become man. "Unless you believed in vain" stands for "except if you believed in vain." For I tell you that if you do not hold fast, it is clear that you believed in vain.

The word of the gospel is the resurrection from the dead, which began with Christ's resurrection. If God had not wished death to be destroyed, he would not have become man. So if you do not hold fast to what you heard but have thrown it away, it is clear that you believed in vain. The word "unless" stands for "except."
He said "first of all" in the sense of "before everything else I handed this on to you."

"First of all" means before everything else. He is saying: I did not hand on an argument of my own, but what I received from the Scriptures. And he was assured by seeing it himself: Christ died and rose, and called him from heaven.
How could he have been buried if he did not have flesh, as the heretics say?
Meaning "more than five hundred."

One untimely born is a child expelled before it is fully formed and before it has spent its proper time in the womb, so that it cannot live. Infants are formed in the womb, and in the same way souls were formed beforehand for piety under the law, and then reborn of water and Spirit. But Paul persecuted the church; he was not formed to completion under the law, since he was a persecutor. That is why he called himself one untimely born, and he adds next: "because I persecuted the church of God."

Infants expelled before they are fully formed in the womb are called untimely births. Under the law souls were formed beforehand for piety, and then reborn of water and Spirit. Paul, however, persecuted the church, as one who had not been properly formed under the law. So he rightly calls himself one untimely born.
He is the least among the apostles because they did not persecute but believed, while he says: I persecuted.
Although he was a persecutor, by God's foreknowledge he received such great grace. That is why he also labored more than the others.
He is saying: I did not receive much grace for nothing. I used it for the preaching, laboring more than all of them.
This means: I did not receive the grace for nothing, for I have labored.
It cannot be that Christ rose while the rest of us no longer rise. Rather, it is agreed that Christ died and rose for no other reason than our resurrection.

He is saying: if Christ has not been raised, you believed in vain that your sins are forgiven, since the one who forgives them has not been raised. But if Christ has been raised, as indeed he has, then clearly sins are forgiven, and there will be a resurrection of the dead.

We are to be pitied because we do not pursue the good things of this life. We despise the goods of the present life, and willingly humble ourselves in poverty, in self-control and in other ways, hoping for other things. If that hope is false, how are we not to be pitied, since we pursue the opposite of what we pray for? By adding "only" he showed that piety is good for the present life as well.

We ask what kind of death they say the Savior underwent, and what kind of resurrection. If both were mere appearance, then the faith of Christians comes down to appearance. But if his death was real, his resurrection was real too. Let them say what kind of death or what kind of resurrection. Is death the taking on of flesh? Then the Lord had flesh. And if he had flesh, he also died. And if he died, he also rose, and Christ became the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep; so our bodies too have been raised. But what kind of death should I take it to be? Dying to sins? But he himself says, "The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me." Suppose he did die as a sinner, the death of sin, since he took away the sin of the world. By that argument he has not risen to this day, for he is always a sinner, since he is always taking away the sin of the world. And what kind of resurrection of the Lord does Paul mean? Release from the flesh? Then he had flesh. Release from sins? Then the same argument applies as before. Besides, if Christ is the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, then whatever kind of resurrection we grant ourselves, we must grant the same kind to the Savior. So what kind of resurrection do we receive? Release from the flesh? Then the Lord too had flesh. Release from sins? Then the Lord too had sins from which he was released. So on every side [?] from the sequence and force of the apostle's words.

Suppose the resurrection belongs to the soul, and its resurrection means release either from the flesh or from sins. Then how have those who fell asleep in Christ perished, if they were righteous? If they are in Christ, they are not sinners. And if resurrection is release from the flesh, the soul is immortal and has not perished. You see that he is speaking of our flesh, which falls asleep in Christ when we die, provided the one who departed was upright.
By adding "only" he showed that the present life is good too. In this life we practice piety, and in that life we receive the rewards.

Let those who accept these words say through what man death came, or what kind of death it is. Through Adam? But it was the soul that sinned and the body that was condemned. Next: "As in Adam all die," and so on. He is speaking of the sentence passed on the matter, since not everyone is said to have died: Enoch and Elijah are alive, and some will be found alive at the Savior's coming.

He said "all" because of the sentence and because all are liable to it, since not all have died, for example Enoch and Elijah, and some will be found alive at his coming. By "in Adam" he means "because of Adam," just as "in Christ" means "because of Christ." So in Adam we die, clearly in the body, and in Christ they will be made alive, clearly in the body. If souls were alive before Christ, and after Christ only souls are alive again, what did the dispensation add?

By "order" he means the order of the righteous and the unrighteous. Here, by "those who belong to Christ," he does not mean the faithful in particular but everyone, because all belong to Christ. At his coming there will be the resurrection of all, and then also the end: the drowning of both death and the devil. For that is the end of the world.

He calls it the kingdom not because it is his own, but because it is the one the evil one seized when he overthrew Adam and those descended from him. In handing this kingdom over to the Father he will not be shut out of it, for the Son reigns together with the Father. The phrase about reigning does not mark a time limit. It adds emphasis, as if someone were to say, “I must live virtuously until I achieve righteousness.” He does not mean that once he has achieved it he will no longer live in righteousness. He means that righteousness is to be achieved through virtuous effort. In the prophets too, “until” does not always mark a time limit but adds emphasis, as in the Old Testament where he says, “I am, I am, until you grow old.” He does not say that the old age of the aged sets a limit to his existence. He means: even if you grow old, I am; I do not grow old along with you but always exist. So here too “until” signifies an end [?]. What he means is this: his kingdom will not be interrupted in the meantime, and believers will not fall away [?] until what he has purposed is accomplished, and once he has accomplished it he will reign for ever.
If the bodies remain dead, he says, and do not rise, why are we baptized on behalf of these dead, as though they will rise and be judged, and receive forgiveness of sins so as not to be condemned?
As far as human beings were concerned, he says, I fought with wild beasts, but God saved me.

The Greeks object that a seed split in two no longer sprouts, and that in the same way a man who has had his foot cut off, or whose body has been mutilated altogether, will not rise again. They do not realize that it is not one nature being set beside another. What is in play is the power of the Maker. Who gave the seed its nature to sprout and its power to germinate? Was it not God? Who makes the seed first die and then rise? Is it not God? So the one who gave the grain its power to germinate has also given our bodies the strength to rise again.
I did not bring in the body of crops and the body of human beings as though they were alike. I brought them in to show the creative power.

He does not mean that the other kinds of flesh rise. He is using an illustration. By “heavenly bodies” he means the sun and the moon, and he goes on to make his point: “So also is the resurrection of the dead.” You see that what came first was an illustration, and now he has supplied the thing the illustration stood for.
The heavenly bodies are the sun and the moon.

By the “natural body” he means the body put to death by the sin of the soul. By the “spiritual body” he means the body raised by the power of the Spirit. That body will no longer live by the weakness of the soul, which cannot keep the body together, but by the power of the Spirit, which carries it over into immortality.
This is what Moses says: “And the man became a living soul.” “The second man became a life-giving spirit.” This is what the Gospel says: “For what has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.”
Man is “from the earth” by nature, but he is “of dust” by choice. By the one “from heaven” he means Christ; not by likeness, or [?] eternity comes from the resurrection.

The followers of Valentinus and Marcion, the disciples of Photinus and those of Apollinarius all seize on this passage, but the text refutes every one of them. Let me ask: did the man of dust from the earth have a soul or not? They will not deny it. And the Lord from heaven had a body from the earth. Again I ask: why does he call the first man “from the earth, of dust,” but the Lord “from heaven”? And why does he then say, “As was the man of dust,” and no longer mention earth but say, “so are those who are of dust”? Clearly it is because “from the earth” refers to nature, while “of dust” refers to choice. When he comes to “as was the man of dust” and is accusing those who have lived badly, he no longer mentions nature or “from the earth.” He no longer calls the Lord “from heaven” but “heavenly,” because the spiritual too were from the earth. “As was the man of dust, so are those who are of dust; and as is the heavenly one, so are those who are heavenly.” If some deny that the Lord from heaven took on flesh because he is from heaven, they are forced to deny that the heavenly ones took on a body too, since “as was the man of dust, so are those who are of dust.” So the passage cannot stand at all if it is understood in any other way than this: he spoke of the nature, which is why he says “from the earth.” Both the heavenly ones and those called “of dust” come from this nature, but they are not both “of dust.” We must notice, then, that it is the Lord who is said to be from heaven, not the heavenly ones, and that it is the heavenly ones who are from the earth, not the Lord from heaven. By “the image of the man of dust” he means an earthbound way of living, and by “the image of the heavenly one” the heavenly way of life. He means: as we imitated Adam's disobedience, let us also imitate the obedience of the Son of God by obeying.

Many heretics, out of great folly, drag this verse in against the resurrection. But he did not say that flesh and blood will not rise. He said they will not inherit the kingdom of God. He shut them out of the kingdom of the Son of God, not out of the grace of the resurrection. What he means is this: flesh, as long as it is flesh, does not inherit, and blood, as long as it is blood, does not inherit. As long as flesh is flesh it is perishable. But once it has put on imperishability and laid aside the weakness of the flesh, it becomes something else, namely imperishable.
He has proved what he said before this. He calls the kingdom “imperishability,” and he calls mortality in this age “perishability.” Opposites do not become heirs of their opposites.

He has shown that there are many trumpets. By mentioning the last one he also implied the first ones. “And the dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed.” If the dead are imperishable, clearly they too will be changed. Why then does he need to add “and we shall be changed”? Surely he spoke of imperishability as common to all, while “we shall be changed” here hints at a change for the better. That is why he said “we,” meaning the righteous.

By saying this and pointing to the body, he hemmed in the heretics who say that there is a resurrection of the soul and not of the flesh. These people are impious about the divine plan of salvation itself. They think Christ took on flesh in appearance and not in truth, which is senseless. If he had no flesh, what was it that died, was buried and rose? And if these things happened in appearance, then we too die only in appearance. Imperishability, then, is common to all who will be raised, but being changed belongs to the saints alone, and it points to a change for the better. The “we” is superfluous, unless he wants it to refer to the saints, meaning “the righteous who are with us.” Elsewhere too, when he said “we who are alive,” he was referring to the saints around him.
“Collection” refers to the contribution gathered for the relief of the poor.

Earlier, when he rebuked them, he did not rebuke them alone, and now, when he is reconciled with them, he does not write alone either. By taking holy Timothy in with him he shows that the matter can be trusted. And here, by saying “through the will of God,” he showed that the word “through” also applies to the Father.

In the former letter he did not rebuke them alone, and now, when he consoles them, he does not write alone either; by taking holy Timothy in with him he shows that the matter can be trusted. Since he says “from God our Father,” we should know that with respect to begotten beings he is called both God and Father, but with respect to the Son he is called only Father. Christ said “my God and your God” while he was in the flesh.

This is the glory with which he glorifies God, and the titles by which he names him already announce the reconciliation in advance: “Father of mercies and God of all comfort.” With respect to begotten beings he is called both God and Father, but with respect to the Son he is confessed as Father only.

Since he is writing to people in affliction, he fittingly begins with God's mercies and comfort, holding out good hopes to them. If God is the Father of mercies, he will surely comfort those who are persecuted and afflicted for his sake.
When God comforts and consoles, he does not consolation in small measure.
He announces these things beforehand because he was about to use this appeal to call back the man who had been condemned for his sin.

Our affliction becomes your consolation: if the apostles are afflicted, how much more the rest. Or he also means this: even if we are afflicted by people for the sake of your salvation, we suffer this because we preach Christ to you.
If we receive consolation from God for your sake, it is so that we may be equal to the task of comforting you, and so urge you to bear the same sufferings that we also endure.
I hope that you, as you endure the same things I do, will likewise receive comfort from God.
He does not recount the afflictions that befell him in Asia to show off. He does it to prepare them, like athletes, for enduring sufferings.
That is, so that we despaired even of life.

A “sentence” is the verdict handed down by a judgment. As far as it depended on ourselves, then, we had received the sentence of death. Through it we are taught not to trust in ourselves but in God, who saves even those who have given themselves up for lost.

He prays to escape those plotting against him, not because he loves his body, but so that he may serve the gifts given to him. He wants thanks to be given by many people now, and through many who are yet to come, for the preaching that saves them. By saying “through many” he pointed to the teaching of those yet to come. The words “thanks may be given on your behalf” mean “for the gift which we ourselves have received.”
This is our boast: that our conscience bears witness that we preach rightly.

He does hold the wisdom of outsiders to be merely natural, but here he hints that he did not use speech the way outsiders do. His motive for preaching was not a fleshly one, such as getting something from them.

When we were with you we taught you nothing different from what we are now writing to you. We taught these very things, which you are also reading, plain and unadorned as they are. So you also recognize that our speech is unskilled, but that the power working to bring about faith is God's.

Paul calls the Corinthians his boast because of what he achieved by preaching to them. And on the day of Christ he is the boast of the Corinthians themselves, since they have glory, as it were, from having received the preaching.

I hope that you will understand fully, since you have already understood in part, that on the day of the Lord we are your boast, just as you are ours. We who preached take pride in our success, and you take pride in having believed the preaching.
I was not planning to come for any fleshly reason but for God's sake, and planning to come for God's sake is not fickleness.

When I planned to come to you, I did not promise you this out of rashness or fickleness. What I plan, I do not plan according to the flesh; I plan spiritual things. And it is fitting that someone who plans spiritual things should never prove false, so that with him yes is yes and no is no.

Whether I come or not does not depend on me, but resolving to come does. If the preaching had been both yes and no, my plan to come to you would rightly have been both yes and no as well. But if the word is true, the plan is wholly true too.
I trust in God that nothing we have preached is false.
For the Son of God, our Lord Jesus, did not prove a liar either.

Through Christ we send up the Amen to God the Father, and we have received our firm footing in Christ through God. By saying “who sealed us” he showed that we belong to God and have been separated from the evil one. Shepherds too put a seal on their flocks to tell their own animals apart from other people's. By saying “pledge” he indicated that we have received a small first installment of knowledge, while the full amount is still owed to us. A pledge is a part of the whole.
Since there were many charges against them, he did not want to come and condemn them.
The statement is elliptical. He means: I wanted to come to you, but not as one who is lord and master of your faith.
Whether you stumble depends on you, but correcting you when you stumble depends on us, so that we may become co-workers of the joy that is according to God.

Believing depends on you, and correcting those who stumble depends on us, so that we may become co-workers of the grace of God. He means joy according to God, for the apostle would not have worked with them toward worldly joy.
By saying “in faith” he implied that they were falling short in works. So, since their faith was fruitless and still incomplete, he says that he is a co-worker with them.
That is why I did not come: not to spare you grief, but to spare myself, and so as not to condemn some of you for what you are doing.

You and I do not grieve each other for the same reasons. You grieve me by sinning, and I grieve you by rebuking you. But the one who is grieved brings gladness, since it seems he is grieved because he has taken it to heart. The one who is not grieved clearly did not even care that he was rebuked. So even if I grieve you, I am doing something fitting, something that leads to my gladness over the good it does you.

I wrote this, that it was to spare you that I did not come, at the end of this letter, where it says, “lest when I come God humble me.” And I wrote for this reason: so that I might find you corrected and be glad, and so that you would not be grieved. I did not say this with my own interest in view, but yours. I know that if you see me rejoicing you rejoice, and if you see me in pain you are in pain too.
I wrote these things so that, if you want me to come to you, you may correct your faults beforehand.

He shows that he makes their very faults his own, and by his mourning and tears he revealed the love he has for them. By saying “I wrote to you,” he means: not simply so that you would be grieved, but so that joy according to God might follow the grief.

If someone has grieved me, though I love him, he has grieved not me alone but, in part, you as well, “so as not to overburden” by saying “Christ too.” He kept silent and did not say “and Christ too,” so as not to weigh heavily on them by saying it.
By “punishment” he means the condemnation passed by the majority.
To forgive him this.
You obeyed me in condemning him; obey me also in calling him back now that he has been condemned.
Forgive him this, he says, for you know that whatever you forgive this man, I too want to forgive. By this he shows that, out of his affection for them, he wants to be of one mind with them.

He appears to have been displeased with the believers in Troas because they did not make much of Titus or keep him there until Paul arrived, but let him leave, as people slack in their faith. So he passed them by as unworthy, to discipline them, even though a door had been opened and no one was shutting out the preaching. Or he passed them by for this reason too: he could easily set things right there later when he visited, since there was nothing to stand in the way.

That is, to him who makes public the insults and hardships we suffer for Christ. He acknowledges a greater grace in being counted worthy to be led in triumph for Christ's sake. He also says this because of the Corinthians, for he was afraid that they might give way under the afflictions they were enduring and fall away from salvation.

Idolaters are in spiritual death because of the ignorance and hardness in them, and they fall into a second death by not accepting the preaching of the gospel. But those who came to the beginnings of the knowledge of God through the training of the law are in a sense already in life. Even so, if they believe in Christ, they receive the fragrance of the knowledge of the Father, from life to life.
A little further on he interprets this passage differently.

To accomplish such things belongs to those who are the aroma of Christ: not to ordinary people, but to those who serve God sincerely. He does not say these things about himself, since that would be offensive. But by what he adds, “for we are not like the many,” he pointed to himself.

By “peddling” the word he means either mixing it with circumcision and sabbath-keeping, or some people treating godliness as a source of gain. “I say that I speak from sincerity,” and he says that he has this very sincerity from God and not from his own power. He also gives another sense: we speak from sincerity because we speak from God, not playing games with these matters but proclaiming God's revelation.

He says this because there were also false apostles who treated the message of godliness as a source of gain. Then he adds “from sincerity,” meaning: we are not playing games with these matters, [he says,] but proclaiming the revelation from God, without peddling the word of God. The word of God is peddled when it is mixed with circumcision and the sabbath, and when people think that godliness is a source of gain.

From this point he wants to show how far the law falls short of grace. He does not want any of the circumcision party to shame the believers from among the Gentiles with the prestige of Moses and the prophets and so bring them over to keeping the law.

That is, this faith and life of yours becomes a letter to everyone and a sign of our preaching. “Written with the Spirit,” he says, that is, by the working of the Holy Spirit. By saying “tablets of stone” and “hearts of flesh,” he shows how far grace surpasses the law: as far as a heart is better than a lifeless tablet. He also shows how much better the grace of the Spirit is than the law, and how much higher the preaching of the apostles is than the ministry of the prophets.
“From ourselves” means “from one another.”

By “the letter” he means the law, and by “the Spirit” he means grace. The law gives commands but does not help, so it weighs people down and kills those who cannot fulfil it by the punishment it brings. The Spirit makes people clean from sin and supplies gifts, and so it plainly leads to life.

And yet the glory was not on the tablets but on Moses' face, as he himself says next: “because of the glory of his face, which was fading.” But because he does not want to argue against the prophet Moses, he calls the law “Moses” and directs his argument against it, showing that the grace given to Moses is less than the grace of the apostles. “But if the ministry of death.” He calls Moses the ministry of death, and he calls the law death, because when it was disobeyed it brought about death. The law is not discredited by this, however, for the apostles too are called “an aroma of death to death.”

By “the ministry of the Spirit” he means the apostles, and by “the ministry of death” he means Moses. But to spare Moses he mentions tablets: Moses brought tablets down from the mountain, while the apostles, sent out into the world, brought the Spirit.

And yet the glory was not on the tablets but on Moses' face. Here, wanting to speak about Moses as well, he points to Moses by means of the law. He calls the law itself a minister of death, because the law put to death those who did not fulfil it. He does not say this to discredit it, for he also called the apostles an aroma of death because of those who do not obey the preaching. The aroma of death is the threat of hell, which brings eternal death on unbelievers, and the aroma of life is the preaching of the kingdom, which sends those who follow the teaching on to eternal life. The aroma runs ahead of the thing itself.

He calls Moses a minister of condemnation and death, because in the law he condemned those who did not obey, and he calls the apostles the ministry of the Spirit. Moses brought down the law, but the apostles carried the Spirit to the world.

The glorified letter of the law, when examined beside the surpassing glory of the Spirit, has not been glorified. No one could say it has been glorified in this respect, when it is compared with what surpasses it.
He showed that the law had to cease and be set aside, while the grace of the Spirit, brought in to take its place, remains.

“Since then we have such a hope.” Hope that is seen is not hope. He showed that grace remains, and even after the resurrection receives further increase, in contrast to the sons of Israel not being able to gaze at the end of what was fading. Just as they could not look at the glory ... [?], so they could not look at the end of the law either, that is, at the fact that the law will cease. Immediately he says, “To this day they have a veil.” The end of the law comes when the veil is lifted and they behold the glory of the Spirit, and see that the law is abolished in Christ, that is, through faith in him.
What hope? That the grace of the Spirit is not abolished as the law is, but remains even after the resurrection.

Because of the blessed hope that the grace of the Spirit endures, we teach with boldness. We do not imitate Moses' arrangements. By the veil over his face he signified that the Jews cannot gaze at the truth and grasp that the law will come to an end and be set aside.
The veil remains and does not let them even see that the law is abolished now that Christ has come.

Moses wore the veil while speaking to the Jews, but when he turned back to the Lord he took it off. In the same way the Jews today, after they have read the law and handed back the book, take off the veil, as though Moses had turned back to the Lord. So if you turn away and come to the Spirit, your veil is taken away, just as it was when Moses turned back to the Lord.
Whoever has been counted worthy of the Spirit of the Lord has been set free from the condemnation of the law, for the gifts are worked through the Spirit. And the gift is for those who are worthy.

We apostles, he says, are seen by people with unveiled face. By saying “we all,” he shows that the Spirit's kindness is shared by all. Moses' glory could not be approached by the Israelites, but the glory of God can be approached by us. Having made ourselves firm in faith and purified ourselves, we behold the glory of God as in a mirror. That is, we both see it and take on in our souls, as in a mirror, the imprint of the image of the Spirit's glory. We are transformed from knowledge of the law to spiritual grace. Or it should be understood this way: from the glory of the Spirit at work in us we come, plainly, to the glory of adoption as sons. “Just as” means “inasmuch as it comes from the Lord, the Spirit.” Note that he called the Holy Spirit Lord, not the Son of God. One person looks into a mirror, and the mirror takes on the likeness of the one looking. It is the same with the Spirit. Those who behold the glory of Christ as in a mirror themselves carry away a certain likeness, from glory to glory; that is, they draw to themselves and receive the glory of the spiritual image.

We are transformed from knowledge of the law to spiritual grace, and from glory, not the glory of the law but that of the Spirit, to the glory of adoption as sons. For when we have received the washing of baptism, we come into adoption as sons.
He means the [surpassing power] of grace, not that of the law; for through the abundance of grace we trample afflictions underfoot.

The hidden things of shame are the base and shameful deeds that those who commit them are eager to hide because they are ashamed; for base deeds have no share in openness, but escape notice in the dark.
Even if the gospel is veiled, it is veiled to unbelievers; it is not as under the law, when the glory of Moses' face was veiled from all Israel.

If one reads "the god of this age" as a single phrase, then "blinded" follows in natural sequence. But if one reads "God blinded" by transposition of words, as in "God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that do not see," and "I hardened Pharaoh's heart," then it is to be understood according to the explanation already given.

Just as he is called the ruler of this age, not because he is a ruler by nature, but because those who were deceived made him their ruler by obeying him, so too he is called the god of this age, not because he is truly a god, but because he is named a god by what the nations say and think, just as the belly is called the god of gluttons.

If we had preached ourselves, he says, one might have suspected that we were falsifying the word; but if we preach Jesus Christ and his glory, there is no deceit at all in the preaching, according to the saying: "Whoever seeks his own glory is not true, but whoever seeks the glory of the one who sent him is true."
If we were preaching ourselves, one might suspect that we were falsifying the word; but if we preach Christ and his glory, there is no deceit at all in the preaching.

"In the face of Jesus Christ" means "through Jesus Christ," through him. "For the illumination of the knowledge": because this knowledge was not discovered by reasoning but was set forth through revelation.

It means that through Jesus Christ he shone in our hearts, and the knowledge was not discovered by reasoning but made known through revelation and illumination; for a human being clothed in mere flesh could never have attained it.

By these words and those that follow he shows that God does not allow us to be tested beyond what we can bear. For even if we are afflicted by our persecutors, we are not so hemmed in as to have no escape or way out anywhere; for God gives room to those who are afflicted for the sake of godliness. That is why David also says: "In affliction you gave me room."
We always carry about the dying, in that we are always in danger for Christ's sake, since we share in Christ's sufferings.
The Lord was handed over to death for our sake, and we for our own sake are handed over because of Jesus, so that we may come to share in his life.
The apostles were in danger because of the preaching, but they preached so that those who believe might live; and this is what "but life in you" means.

Since, he says, there was a spirit of slavery in the law, but a spirit of adoption in grace. Having said that we have the same spirit that David also had, he added "of faith": the same spirit of faith, not of the slavery of the law.

Having, he says, the same spirit as David, who spoke in accordance with faith, as he said: "I believed, therefore I spoke." Then, having said "spirit," he added "of faith"; for this alone is common to the New and the Old, since in the law there was a spirit of slavery, but in grace a spirit of adoption.

If deaths and dangers and trials pursued him, how is the affliction light? How is it momentary? For the trials stayed with him and hounded him into old age. How, then, is the affliction of the saints light? Clearly, when it is weighed against the glory of the age to come and against the good things laid up for the righteous; for compared with these even the heaviest trials appear light to me. And the afflictions are not simply light, but exceedingly so, since afflictions fall far short of the greatness of the glory; for a great body is also heavy. Or else he said "weight" by a metaphor taken from scales; for when glory is weighed against afflictions it is found to be very heavy indeed. By "momentary" he means temporary; for even if what afflicts and grieves us lasts long, it appears temporary compared with the endlessness of the glory.

"The house of the tent": not the tent but the house; for our dwelling here comes to an end, but the tent rises again. By "house" he meant our way of life, both the mortal one and the one we await. In what follows, however, he shows that by "dwelling" he means corruption and incorruption.

By "the house of the tent" he means the body. Even if it is destroyed, he says, in trials and dangers for Christ's sake, we shall put it off like a perishable house, the least of things made by hands. But we shall find in the heavens another house, which God provides, imperishable and not made with hands. By these words he indicates both the mortal life and the immortal one.

By "to be clothed over" he shows that the perishable flesh rises again and puts on immortality over itself; for "clothing over" is said of a garment worn on top of another. He speaks of two houses, the mortal one and the one we await, and of two dwellings, corruption and incorruption, because from the one we are released and the other we put on over ourselves. By "the dwelling from heaven" he means the incorruption that comes from the heavens, inasmuch as it is not made by hands but is a gift of God.
All, righteous and unrighteous alike, put on incorruption. But if someone is handed over to punishment, he is no better off than one who is naked.
He means what follows: that we wish to put on incorruption over the body, not to strip off the body itself into corruption. That is why he added: "so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life."
"For this very thing": clearly, for becoming imperishable.
It means: being convinced that while we are at home in the body, that is, while we are still living in the flesh in this world.

Through faith we hope in God, for his form is not visible to us. But we believe this: that we shall depart to him, when we shall see him as far as it is possible for a human being to see God. For Moses too saw bodily, and the angels see as far as it is possible for them to see; for no one has ever seen God, and every creature falls short of the sight of God.

If you are pleasing to him here, you will beyond dispute be more pleasing there, no longer struggling but having the security of pleasing him. It is also possible that "we walk by faith, not by sight" was said about the incarnation of God the Word, since Paul himself was not among those who had seen the Lord in the flesh before the Passion.
Those who please people and do not boast for the sake of piety itself evidently boast in outward appearance before people; for the heart is searched by God.

He calls boasting "being beside ourselves." We boast so that he may be glorified; we keep silent about our boasting, which he calls "being in our right mind," so that we may teach you not to boast. He calls it "being beside oneself" when someone who ought to avoid boasting is compelled to boast.

By "being beside ourselves" he means boasting about one's way of life; for boasting belongs to those who are beside themselves, moderation to those in their right mind. So we are often compelled to be beside ourselves and to boast, so that God may be glorified through us. But we strive to be in our right mind and to be moderate, so that we may teach you too not to boast. He calls it "being beside oneself" when someone who ought to speak [?] is compelled to resort to boasting.

Though we wish to keep silent, we are compelled to boast, constrained by the love of Christ, so that he may be glorified. "All have died": he means the faithful, who have been put to death to the world both through baptism and through their way of life. "And they no longer live for themselves": for if I lived for myself, I would not boast; but since I live for Christ, for his sake I keep silent, if need be, for your benefit, and for his sake I also boast, so that he may be glorified.

Whether we are beside ourselves, he says, or in our right mind for you, we do everything because of the love of Christ. Now one who dies for others frees from death those already condemned, and as far as it depended on us we were dead, if one died for all. Therefore all died, as far as the condemnation is concerned. He means the faithful, who through baptism were put to death to the world, no longer living for themselves but for Christ; for Christ, having died for all and paid the common debt, made the world his debtor.

"So from now on we know no one according to the flesh." Since circumcision, and "eat this" and "do not eat that," and the Sabbath belong to the flesh, he says that we of the faithful know no one according to the flesh. But since the fact that the Lord was circumcised and kept the Sabbath was a stumbling block, he says this at the right moment, to help those under the law. "But now we no longer ... know this" [?]; for he does not want us to live according to the law.

This is said not only with regard to putting desires to death, but also with regard to no longer obeying the law. For even if Christ was circumcised and came under the observances of the law, that is, even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him so. For when he was among human beings, he lived as a man, fulfilling the law in his life; but having died and risen imperishable, he abolished the things of the law and showed the way of the heavenly life. That is why those who are baptized, as having died, put to death bodily ways of life, and, imitating the pure conduct of the heavens, join themselves to God in their hearts.

Whoever lives in Christ and is baptized is a new creation, no longer living according to the law but according to the new grace of the Spirit. For whether you speak of law or of grace, all things are from God; for we do not say that the law is not from God, even if it has come to an end.
He says that the preaching is a ministry of reconciliation, through which, by believing, we shall be reconciled to God.

It should be understood like this: that God was reconciling the world to himself in Christ. So it should be punctuated like this: that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, that is, through Christ.

Now we act as ambassadors in Christ's place, God making his appeal to you through us. Then he also shows that he is grieved on account of those who keep the law; for "on behalf of Christ," he says, not on behalf of the law. And God makes his appeal through us as through Christ, whose ministers and servants we are.

Here he showed how grieved he is on account of those who contentiously insist on keeping the law; for by keeping the law, he says, we have become sinners. Christ became sin in order to free us from sin. And God has provided these things: accept the reconciliation, giving up the keeping of the legal observances.

He entrusted to the apostles not only the task of exhorting but also of working together and toiling with people for their salvation, so that they might sincerely receive the grace that comes from God.
He lays down endurance first as an unbreakable foundation; once it is in place, it is easy to build every commandment upon it.

The weapons of righteousness for the right hand are holding fast to good works, and for the left, abstaining from evil works; and through both of these righteousness is achieved. For it is clear that when one is lacking, the other is rendered useless.
"Through glory" refers to those who receive the word and admire it; "dishonor" to those who insult the believers. The same explanation applies to what follows.

Having said "You are not restricted by us," he means that we do not restrict you in the saving teaching, nor by any shortcoming on our part; for our heart has been opened wide and our mouth opened for teaching. So you too, in return, open wide your minds and receive the teaching; for your heart is not open enough to receive my teachings. So you are restricted by your own doing, being unable to receive further instruction.

Accept us when we speak, so that you may suffer no loss through us. For if I had kept silent, he says, and not rebuked you, you would not have been grieved; and if you had not been grieved, you would have suffered loss by not repenting.
I rejoice, he says, in your afflictions, because they are not worldly but spiritual. And next he recalls the things that happened to him in Asia for Christ's sake.

And yet he did write for this reason. But, as it seems and as the outcome showed, "I was not writing for this reason, but so that your zeal and obedience might be shown"; so that under the pretext of one thing, another came to light.
He was refreshed in this, that they obeyed his teaching.

In the very thing, he says, in which they are sorely afflicted by persecution, they rejoice all the more, and their deep poverty overflowed into the wealth of their generosity. The apostle bears witness to the Macedonians that, though poor, they were lavish in doing good, so that the Corinthians too might be roused to bear fruit.

The eagerness of the Macedonians to do good urged us to ask Titus to come to you, so that he might urge you too to bear fruit. And he said "this grace too" because they had received from him the grace of teaching.
By "of others" he means the Macedonians.

This should be connected with "we have sent with him the brother who is praised in the gospel," so that they might be able to administer the large and generous gift from the Gentiles, taking precautions and guarding ourselves, lest anyone blame us for hindering the good work done for the saints.
In the sight of the Lord it is good to serve in doing good; in the sight of people it is good not to be blamed or slandered in the administration of so generous a gift.

Unlike the soldiers of the world, who receive wages, we do not preach for the sake of receiving wages. "And being ready to punish every disobedience, once your obedience is complete." Since I knew that some are persuaded by words and exhortation, I did not wish at once to use the severity I intend to use against some, since it was not yet clear who would obey by word alone. So first I rebuked them by word, so that those who correct themselves by this means might be taught, and those who do not obey the word but need the severity of deeds might be exposed.

Knowing that some are persuaded just by hearing, I do not wish to use severity yet, but only once those who obey have become evident, so that it may be shown who are those instructed by word and who are those who need correction.

Examine each person carefully according to the merit of his conduct. He has the apostles in view here: since he was about to refute those of the circumcision, and they put forward Peter, James and John, "Take care," he says, "that the rank of persons does not prevent you from seeing the truth."

We write these things not in imitation of those who commend themselves (for that is not good); for they do not understand that they measure themselves by themselves and cannot be compared with anyone else; for compared with others they are nothing.
We do not, like insignificant people, boast of greater things beyond our own measure; for we did come all the way to you and preached the word.

They boast of our labors, but we do not; rather we boast lawfully, according to the rule and the measure assigned to us, hoping, as your faith grows, to preach the gospel in the regions beyond you as well. By "rule" he means having reached as far as them so far.
Even if we boast, it is not as though we succeed by our own understanding, but by the grace of the Spirit.

You died to the law, he says, and have come to belong to another husband, to him who rose from the dead. How then is she a pure virgin, having been married before? Because, having been reborn through the washing of regeneration and passed into another life, she is rightly called a pure virgin.

Christianity is confirmed by faith in Christ and the illumination of the Spirit. If, then, you did not receive these from us, you would be right to seek out those who still wish to live according to the law.

He does not say this to reproach the Corinthians, but he is refuting those who treat the preaching as a trade. That is why he says: I do not cease to boast that I have not made the preaching a trade as they have; for I neither received anything from you nor do I receive anything, not because I do not love you (for I do love you), but in order to cut off the pretext of my accusers, so that whether they boast falsely or truly, they may be shown up, just as we too have been shown openly.

This is strong proof that the soul is immortal; for if he had known that it was mortal, he would not have been in doubt whether he saw the vision outside the body or in the body. By "as far as the third heaven" he meant the third part of the distance; for if he had ascended through three heavens, he would surely have heard the unspeakable words there and not in paradise. And let no one think that paradise is above heaven; for it was planted in the east, on earth, in the place called Eden, from which Adam too was formed, as Moses relates. By "weaknesses" he means the persecutions, not a bodily ailment, as some think.

Many suspect that he had a pain in his head, but in truth he means the persecutions, since the trials came about through the working of the devil. He called the trial that serves the devil "an angel of Satan," by analogy with the angels who serve God. "Was given" must be understood as meaning by God's permission, as also in the case of Job; for God does not give evils.
You have apostolic grace; do not seek to exercise it without trials as well; for my power is made perfect in persecutions and afflictions.

Unless, then, you can charge me with this: that I took nothing from you for my keep, bearing my want without complaint. If you think I did wrong in this, forgive me and pardon me this wrong that you think you have suffered from me.
He solemnly declares this to them with regard to his coming to them a second and a third time for the sake of the preaching.

Just as Christ is said to have become sin and a curse, though he was neither sin nor a curse, but made our ills his own in order to rescue us from them, so too here he is said to have been crucified in weakness, not his own weakness, but the weakness he took on himself for our sake, arranging everything for our benefit.

After the preaching had been received among the Gentiles, some of those from the circumcision went out and tried to persuade the Gentiles to live like Jews.
