The first dispute about this appears to have taken place in Antioch, when the apostles wrote that the Gentiles were not to be subject to the law, but were to abstain from food sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what is strangled, and from sexual immorality; for so it seemed good to the Holy Spirit. But this sickness took hold of the Galatians, who all with one accord wanted to live like Jews. They were won over by the troublemakers, who said that the other apostles did not prevent those who wished to keep the law.
He shows that it was not Moses who died for the world, nor any other of the prophets. One must not, then, submit to the one who did not save, but to the one who died for us.
"To a different gospel, which is not another," he says; for our gospel and that of the apostles wants you to be free of the law.

Granted, an angel; but why "we" too? When we preached, we preached by the power of the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit does not change its mind. If, then, we say something different, we have abandoned the things of the Spirit. So let even the preacher be accursed if he rejects the preaching.

"Contrary to what you received." It is not that I preached, he says, and you did not receive it; rather, I preached and you received it. I do not regret having preached, and you, for your part, keep what you have received.

"Am I now trying to win over people, or God? Or am I seeking to please people? If I were still pleasing people, I would not be a slave of Christ." As he is about to remind them of his own gospel, he first guards himself, so that they will not think he is flattering them to win them over; for he rebukes them while admonishing them. By saying "still," he made it clear that he once pleased people. Whom did he please? Those from whom he received letters to harm the faithful in Damascus. If, then, he says, I were still pleasing the Jews, I would not have believed in Christ.

What need was there to mention his former way of life in Judaism, except to show that he serves not prejudice but truth? For it was not out of hatred for the law that he took refuge in grace (indeed, he used to defend the law zealously), but having found what is perfect he departed from the law.

Now he shows that he has something more than Peter and those with him; for they were not zealous for Judaism, resisting Christianity, as I was. So do not think that I came to grace out of hatred for the law (for I used to defend the law zealously); rather, I found what is perfect, and I do not put the law on a level with perfect grace.
He does not say this to disparage the apostles, but to mean: I did not take my lead from mortal flesh.

For if no one is justified by works, which involve toil, but by faith, where the ease is great and the righteousness great, how is it not necessary, he says, to leave the law behind and be content with grace? He says one is not justified by works of the law, not that one is not justified by the commandments; for the commandment justifies when it is heeded, but the work was what was hard to accomplish.

The words are addressed to Peter: you abolished these things by the decree sent from you to the people of Antioch and to the whole world. It is unfitting, then, to teach others these things, whose observance you yourself have given up and abolished by your own decree.

The law has its practice and its enjoyment in bodily things: eat this, do not eat that, keep the Sabbath, circumcision. Grace does not want you to win approval through these things. So I died, he says, to these things. What need have I of the law?

"It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me." When I lived for myself, I was under the law. But since Christ lives in me, who is no longer under the law but in the heavens at the right hand of the Father, I do not set aside the one who lives in me.

"And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith," for I believe in the Son of God. And if the Son of God, in whom I believe, is at the right hand of the Father, then my citizenship is in the heavens; but the law had its observances among things on earth. So I am not subject to the law.

The law weighed more heavily, and that is why it was called a ministry of death. How then, he says, was it added because of transgressions? Put briefly, it is like this: before the law, the human mind, together with the flesh, was enslaved to sin and loved evil; when the law was given, the mind was instructed, but the flesh was still held captive. Now one who does not know that sin is sin pursues impiety as if it were piety and devotes himself to it all the more zealously, whereas one who knows that it is evil gains at least this: he is aware that he is transgressing and longs to obey God. For this reason the law was given. "A law able to give life" stands for "if a law had been given"; it was not given, he says, against the promises of God, but neither could it hold sway forever.
Even if the law accomplished nothing else, it did at least give knowledge of God. And knowing God made people ready to receive grace.

It is not keeping the law, he says, that makes the Jews who have believed better than those from the Gentiles. Rather, the power of baptism, which grants the putting on of Christ, makes grace common to all alike: barbarians, Greeks, Jews, female, male. He did not mix in female and male without purpose, since as far as the wording went, “one” was all that the point at hand required. He meant that if baptism gathers male and female, who differ, into one grace, how much more Greek and Jew.

Now he wants to show that after grace has come, even if someone thinks he is keeping the sabbath and new moons and feasts according to the law, he is in effect worshipping idols. He is serving the elements that he worshipped when he was a Gentile, only in another way. Nor is he keeping the law, for it has ceased. In calling the elements “poor,” he was not accusing them of being evil. He meant that they cannot make anyone rich and are not sufficient for godliness.

Do not think, he says, that I had some other grievance against you and that this is why I rebuke you. The intensity of his pain forces him constantly to change the form of his speech: now he rebukes, now he exhorts, at one time he accuses, at another he laments. Here, then, he teaches that what he writes, he writes out of affection. “For I have suffered no wrong from you,” he says. On the contrary, he says, he was shown care, and indeed the very greatest care.

“What then was the blessedness?” This means that there was none. Or it can be read like this: which is blessed, keeping the law or living by faith? He had said that those people do not want to emulate you, so as to have the perfection of faith themselves without keeping the law, but want you to emulate them. So he added that he says this not out of envy toward them: “I wish that they too were perfect, having made use of faith. Then nothing would prevent them from being emulated and from imitating us. So you too should do the kind of things that make you worthy of emulation, so that all may imitate you. And do not become like this only when I come, out of respect for me; correct yourselves even when I am not present.”

Here he has used the term loosely, not in the proper sense of allegory. Allegory does not keep to the literal words. It introduces other things, which are indicated by the sequence of thought running through the passage. An example is “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth” in the Song of Songs. There it is not a kiss, or hair, or belly, or thighs, or anything else; one thing is introduced by means of another, and this is the proper form of allegory. Here, however, the history is acknowledged as true, and it has been shown to be a type of what was to come. So what is here called allegory is prophecy through deeds. For some prophecies are made through words only, such as “Behold, the virgin shall conceive in her womb.” Some are made through deeds only, as when Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness. And some are made through both deeds and words, like what was said to Jeremiah: “Take a new loincloth and put it on; then bury it by the Euphrates.” And when it had rotted and been eaten away over time, “Take it from there,” he says. Up to this point the prophecy is through deeds, but what follows is also through words: “So I too put on the children of Israel, and so I helped them; and so I am leading them captive to Babylon, and when they have rotted and decayed I will bring them back from there and restore them.” So here he has called prophecy through deeds “allegory.”

He did not mention Mount Sinai for no reason. He did so because the Hagarenes, who descend from Ishmael, occupy the desert that stretches as far as Mount Sinai. It was on Sinai that the law was given, “bearing children for slavery.” The tablets given on Mount Sinai were brought from there into Israel, and after being moved many times from place to place, they were finally set up in Jerusalem. Therefore he added: “She corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children.” Where there is a promise of land, along with possessions and marriage and human affairs, slavery follows too. But where there is release from earthly cares and bonds, and one’s citizenship is in heaven, freedom comes from that very citizenship.

It is asked why, while drawing them away from the law, he mentions sin. The reason is that the law told them to enjoy plenty. This stirs up desire, which cannot be restrained and so leads to sin. That is why, whenever the law was mentioned, he mentions sin as well. In Romans too, when he mentioned the law and the correction brought by the Lord, he added: “Those who live according to the flesh cannot please God.” Why then were plenty and eating permitted? Because abstaining from evils that everyone acknowledged as evil would not have made progress unless they were allowed to eat and drink. The lawgiver knew that people living in plenty cannot master their pleasures. For the time being, however, he wanted to train the mind, so that it would know what is good, what is evil and what is godly. For he foresaw that the one would come who would add what was lacking to the law, namely, not walking according to the flesh, as Paul says.

This makes clear that many were spending their money unwisely. They provided for those who urged people to keep the law but gave nothing to those who preached Paul’s teaching. That is why he says, “He who sows to his own flesh.” For whoever is subject to the law lives among fleshly things. So whoever provides for a teacher of such things sows only to the flesh.

He did not want to be thought of as championing uncircumcision instead of circumcision, or to give his opponents an opening for slander. So he very aptly added the final point: that neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision. Instead he spoke of a new creation, about which he says elsewhere: “If anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation.” If there is a new creation, he says, do not come under the law. For whoever lives according to the law lives in the world, but whoever lives in Christ has his citizenship in heaven. So “the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”

He wrote to the Romans before he had ever seen them, and in the same way he wrote to the Ephesians, after John had gone before him and laid the foundation of the preaching among them. He timely urges them not to be held captive by the law, since the apostles living in Jerusalem kept the law for the sake of believers from the circumcision. Then, since John had spoken sufficiently about God and had left out nothing of the preaching that leads to the knowledge of God, as far as humans can grasp it, Paul turns to setting out the economy of the incarnation. He clothes it with its own proper greatness, in words worthy of the realities, and so takes on the harder task. For the dignity of the Godhead was its own and was acknowledged by all. But the incarnation looked lowly, and to describe it worthily required spiritual power.

Here too, according to Paul, the word “through” is used of God, and the Father is not lessened by it. He fittingly says “through the will of God,” to show that just as God willed John to be an apostle, so he willed me. He writes this so that what he says may be trusted.

Suppose both “Father” and “Lord” are used loosely. Then the Son would have to be acknowledged as greater than the Father, since one has the name of Father and the other the name of Lord. But the reason for these words is clear. He had said “our Father,” but God is the Father of Christ. The same name was not to be applied both to the Only-begotten and to the faithful, which would either bring the Son down below his nature or raise the faithful above theirs. So, having said “our Father” and shown that this title is given by grace, he added “and the Lord Jesus Christ.” For even though the title is shared, it was not possible for the dignity to be shared as well through a common nature. Otherwise, why is the Father Lord of the faithful, but not Lord of the Son too, if the title was used loosely in both cases?
If, then, the saints were predestined to adoption in Christ, the Son is not adopted. He is Son by nature.
If, according to the rule [?], willing is an activity, what is the “good pleasure” of this willing? For he would not have spoken of a willing of a will.
“To the praise of the glory of his grace.” I have already said that he adorns his own discourse with the dignity of the economy.

The human being who had been formed fell through disobedience, and when humans became impious, the heavenly things were estranged from the earthly. So Christ came and summed up all things. He says the same thing later in another way: “having made peace between the things in the heavens and the things on earth.” For he is our peace, who made both one, Jews and Greeks, through faith in Christ.

Here he clearly treats activity and will as two different things. After saying “of him who works all things according to the counsel,” he said “of his will,” to show that the will is a deliberate judgment. He used these terms to say that whatever someone has confirmed out of good counsel has been decided by judgment.

You too, he says, are among those foreknown. You are made Christ’s own through obedience, through the faith that follows hearing, and through the sealing that follows faith. That sealing is likeness to Christ through receiving a share in the Spirit. From whom did they hear the word of truth? Was it not from John the Evangelist? For he preached there. That is why Paul speaks to them in a loftier way, since they had been trained by John’s teaching.

The redemption belongs to the possession. We are redeemed so that we may be acquired and made God’s own, remembering the blood by which we were redeemed and the whole economy. Clearly he calls him “God” of Christ with respect to Christ’s flesh. For nowhere here did he mention the dignity of the Godhead, only the economy on our behalf, which is acknowledged to belong to the flesh. Scripture often calls the very essence of God “glory.” Since that essence cannot be touched or reached, Scripture named it glory, so that you would not demand an explanation but would worship. Ezekiel was the first to call God’s essence glory. He saw God seated in visions and added: “This is the likeness of the glory of the Lord.” God explains this elsewhere when he says: “I multiplied visions, and by the hands of the prophets I was represented in likenesses.” So what Ezekiel called “glory,” God calls “I.” And Paul says: “who, being the radiance of the glory” (what glory?) “and the exact imprint of his substance.” So here too, “the God of our Lord Jesus Christ” is said with respect to the flesh, but “the Father of glory” with respect to the nature.

“And above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come.” In this age we name thrones, principalities, dominions, authorities, powers, angels and archangels. But there are countless ranks of invisible powers that are unknown to us and so have no names. After the resurrection they will be known, and along with that knowledge they will receive names from us too. That is why he said “and in the age to come.”

“And he gave him as head over all things to the church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.” By this he made clear that by “the fullness of God” he means the body of Christ, that is, the church. Why “fullness”? Because it has been filled with God. Just as he fills all things in all, he says, so too he is filled in the church, since it is the body of Christ. So the church is Christ’s body and God’s fullness.

“Of him who fills all in all.” He is in heaven, that is, working there differently from how he works on earth; and he is on earth, working there differently from how he works in heaven. He is in angels and in the sun, but in each according to its own nature. For Scripture speaks about God on the basis of what we receive from him, not on the basis of what he himself is, since that is beyond comprehension.

“World” is used in two senses: for the created order, and for the wicked company of human beings. Here, however, he has distinguished the two by their names [?]. He calls human wickedness and sin “age,” and the order of the universe “world,” just as he says in Galatians: “so that he might rescue us from the present evil age.” By this he means the present age. So he gave the name “age” to the common apostasy and error of humanity, of which those who now believe in Christ were once also a part.

“According to the ruler of the power of the air, of the spirit.” By this the apostle clearly shows that the devil was not an angel from heaven but an evil spirit of the air. The Lord does say, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven,” but he is not indicating the place from which he fell. Lightning falls swiftly from above, and so he compared the swiftness of the devil’s fall to lightning. He means: as lightning flashes swiftly from heaven, so I saw how swift his fall was.
“That is now at work.” He showed that the devil does not always have power. Rather, human weakness has become his strength.
“Doing the wishes of the flesh and of the thoughts.” This shows that the flesh is not opposed to the soul, for the two agreed together in sin.
“And we were by nature children of wrath.” Just as people are called “sons of Gehenna,” so they are also called “children of wrath.”
Since he said “created,” he means that creation is a making of us into his own. He added “for good works” so that from now on you would build yourself up.
He did not say that they were “nearer” than those who believed from the circumcision, only that they were “near.”

“Having broken down the dividing wall of the fence”: not the fence, but the dividing wall. What is the fence? “I will take away its fence, and it will be plundered”; that is, the protection of the Spirit. And what is the dividing wall? The rule against mixing with the Greeks. The Jews had been forbidden to mix with the Greeks so that they would not fall into idolatry, since they practised idolatry even without that contact. This is what David says: “God makes those of one way to dwell in a house.” For the leaven had to become strong, so that in this way the whole world might be leavened.

By “the law of commandments” he means the established law, which came from the commandments of Moses. “Having abolished it by decrees” means by his own decrees. Among them is “What goes in does not defile a person,” which undid “Eat this, do not eat that.” Another is the ban on giving a certificate of divorce, which ran against divorcing a wife for any reason. Another is “You observe days and months and seasons and years,” which ran against what Moses gave. In general there are many such teachings by which he abolished the law of commandments. He did not abolish the commandments as absurd, but abolished the practice as no longer useful. For the commandments are still honoured even when they are not in force. But from then on, the law, that is, our being under the law of commandments, did harm after grace had come.
For the Greeks turn away from idolatry as impiety, and the Jews from the law as no longer useful, and both are being built up into a new kind of godliness.
“Making peace.” For the law does not want there to be peace. Why? So that bodily peace would not stir up war against godliness.
“So that he might reconcile both to God.” For the Greeks had gone astray, and the Jews had transgressed.

“Having killed the enmity in himself.” The thought is broad, though the wording is brief. As was said before, it was the law that separated Jews from Greeks, and the law was going to come to an end. It came to an end in no other way than when the Lord rose from the dead; for after the law, the church had to be joined to him as to another husband. So he says that in his flesh he killed that enmity by bringing the law to an end.

“And he came and preached peace to you who were far off and to those who were near.” This shows that he does not call the law of Moses impious, as idolatry is. He says that the idolaters are far off and the Jews are near. “Near” shows both that they had a share in godliness and that they did not have it in full. If they had possessed it in full, they would not be near; they would be inside it. And if they had been opposed to it, they would not be near either; they would be far off with the Greeks.

Here he wants to show that he did not force himself on them as if they were strangers who had been taught by others. Having been chosen as herald of the Gentiles, he owed them this demonstration too. And just as the Lord taught John and his companions, so he taught me by revelation. He also hinted that he could have said something deeper, but he measured his teaching to what they could take in.

“So that it might now be made known to the principalities.” This is fitting. For if it had been hidden in God, all the powers were ignorant of it. By “now” he does not mean the time of grace, but the time from when the prophets began to reveal what was to come.

The life of the righteous, he says, is in heaven, but the life of all other humans is on earth. The righteous are not ranked on earth with the living. Those dedicated to God stand apart, like a chosen race. Their family is called heavenly because it is pure, but that of the rest is called earthly because it is defiled. It should be noted that, from what the apostle shows, the name of “Father” did not rise from us up to heaven but came down from above to us, clearly because it is his by nature and not in name only. For what is said loosely must always come after what is natural; and among natural things, what is above comes first and then what is below. It should also be noted that he said “family” (patria), meaning kinship, and not “clan” (phratria). For divine Scripture always calls kinship groups “families.”

He has shaped the phrase rather figuratively into the figure of a cross. For what else could depth and height and breadth and length be but the shape of the cross? In a way he seems to speak of the cross as double, and not without reason. The Lord’s economy is Godhead from above and humanity from below, while the apostolic preaching stretched from north to south and from east to west. He brought together both the Lord’s economy and the apostles’ ministry, and spoke as he did to display the double character of the economy, as if in a double cross. For he could not simply name the directions, up and down, and the line, breadth and length.
“So that you may be filled to all the fullness of God,” that is, the church; for he calls the church “fullness.”

“Awake, O sleeper,” and what follows, we find written nowhere in the Old or the New Testament. What is it, then? At that time there was a gift of both prayer and psalms, with the Spirit prompting them, as he says in Corinthians: “Each of you has a psalm, has a prayer.” And again: “What then is it? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind also; I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the mind also.” Clearly, then, what he quoted was contained in one of these spiritual psalms or prayers.
Someone who buys another person’s slave buys him out and acquires him for himself. Since the present time is enslaved to the wicked, buy it out, so as to use it for godliness.

Since the lamb has been offered, we also eat his body. Food tends to be taken up into the body of the one who eats it. We clearly eat his body spiritually, and it is taken up into our body, and so we become flesh of his flesh and bone of his bones.

Not the mystery, but God. What then does he mean? That the forming of Adam, and of Eve who came from him, and their union became a type of Christ and the church. That is why he says: “We are bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh,” just as Eve came from Adam. So by “but I am speaking about Christ and the church” he refers to the mystery of marriage. He means that the law of marriage and the original creation are a type of Christ and the church. That is why he added:

“Nevertheless, you too, each one of you, should love his own wife as himself.” Why did he say “each one of you”? Because what happened with Adam was a type of the church and Christ. That is why he said: “You too, each of you individually, love.” The mystery of which marriage was a type has come to pass and is true, but the type itself must also be fulfilled, and each man must love his own wife.

If the sword is the utterance of God, and the sword belongs to the Spirit, then the Spirit whose sword it is, is God. And if he called the Holy Spirit the utterance of God, then clearly, just as the Son is the Word of God, so too the Spirit is the utterance of God. By “the sword of the Spirit” he meant the Spirit’s power to punish.

He did not say “praying in the Spirit” without reason. As he says elsewhere, “we do not know how we ought to pray,” but “the Spirit himself intercedes for us,” so that our requests may have nothing fleshly in them. Our requests are spiritual because they are helped by the power of the Spirit.
Whoever is freed, he says, from the corruption that comes from the devil receives the grace of the Spirit in incorruption.

In this letter he is writing to clergy, not laypeople. That is why he did not need much moral instruction. His aim in the letter was to make humility succeed among them. By this very exhortation he shows how strict their lives were in other respects. For it is rare for someone both to sin and to be puffed up. Being puffed up affects those who live best and who, for the most part, are made proud by that very fact.

Everywhere and in every way it is shown that my sufferings and my defences are not useless. Your steadfastness, which comes from your faith, is what I offer as proof. When I am accused and make my defence on account of the believers, of whom you are some, my proof is your steadfastness. When I want to confirm the gospel to anyone, my proof is your steadfastness. When I want to show that I am not enduring chains in vain, my proof is your faith.

“And being found in form as a man.” Here the word “as” (hōs) does not express likeness but emphasis, as in “How [hōs] good God is to Israel” and “How [hōs] I have loved your law, O Lord,” which means “I have loved it greatly.”
“Holding fast to the word of life” means “paying attention to the word of life.” He also writes to Timothy, “Hold to yourself,” meaning “Pay attention to yourself.”

If he counts them loss because of Christ, they were not bad things, for they had been gains. And he said “I have counted”: they were not really loss, but compared with the surpassing excellence of better things, he counts them as loss.

The chaff is part of the stalk, and the stalk and the ear once came from the seed. So this chaff was once most useful for producing the seed. For just as root, stalk and ear come from a seed, so from the faith of Abraham, as from a seed, came the [?] of those under the law, then the stalk of the prophets, and then the ear, which was already proclaiming Christ in secret beforehand. The harvesting and threshing of these took place at the first coming of the Savior, whose winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor. So when the stalk of the law came to an end, circumcision, sabbath-keeping and the rest were separated off like chaff. The pure grain of faith, which had been hidden in the prophetic stalk, was then laid up in the granaries of the Master of all. This word "chaff," then, shows that the law is closely related to grace. Just as the seed could not have come into being without the chaff, so the perfection of grace could not have been achieved without the law.
"Forgetting what lies behind": not because those things are bad. What he means is this: I do not spend my time recalling my past struggles, but in thinking about what I shall accomplish next.
Some say that Euodia was the jailer's wife, and Syntyche her husband.
Much of this letter is hard to understand, because many do not know the occasion of the letter or the apostle's aim. The occasion is this.

Those who had come to faith from among the Greeks had Greeks who were still pagans dragging them away to Greek observances. Those who had come from the Jews had Jews urging them to keep the law, as though grace were incomplete without the law. The argument the Greeks put to them was that it was right to worship angels as well. They said their gods were angels: God, they argued, is great and inaccessible to human beings, and so he supplies his operations to those in need through these angels, as through mediators. "The Scriptures too," they say, "recognize the help of angels. God set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God; Michael is the ruler of the Jews, and the ruler of Persia is another angel." And again: "Behold, the ruler of the Greeks is coming." And Jacob says: "The angel who delivers me." And in Acts, about the apostle Peter: "It is his angel," they say. And the Lord says about the children: "Do not hinder them from coming to me, for their angels continually see the face of my Father who is in heaven." From all these things, some of which they believed and others not, both Jews and Greeks drew their conclusion. They said that the grace that comes through the Lord Jesus was superfluous, since the angels who have existed from eternity were enough to bring to God those who obey. They also said it was a defect to disregard all the observances kept among Jews and Greeks. The apostle's aim in the letter before us is directed against these claims.

It is worth setting out the occasion that we have found from the letter itself. Most people understand many things in the Letter to the Colossians differently, because neither the occasion nor the apostle's aim is well known.

Those who had come to faith from among the Greeks had Greeks who were still pagans wanting to drag them back to Greek observances. They also had Jews trying to persuade those who had come to faith to keep the law, as though grace were incomplete without the law. In addition, both Greeks and Jews were trying to persuade the Colossians to give heed to angels. The Greeks said that their gods were angels: God, they argued, is uncontainable and great and not accessible to human beings, but he supplies his benefits to those who receive them through these angels, as through mediators. The Jews said that God set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God. So too, they said, Michael is the ruler of the Jews, and so too "the ruler of Persia withstood me." And again: "Behold, the ruler of the Greeks was coming." So too Jacob says: "The angel who has delivered me from my youth." In the catholic Acts it is said about Peter: "It is his angel." And the Lord says: "See that you do not despise one of these little ones, for their angels behold the face of my Father who is in heaven." From all these texts, some of which they believed and others not, both Jews and Greeks concluded that the grace that comes through the Lord Jesus Christ was superfluous, since angels had existed from eternity to bring near those who obey. They also held that it was a defect to disregard the observances of both the Greeks and the Jews. Paul's aim is directed against these claims, and these are what he corrects. That is why, right at the beginning, he says:
Notice that within a few lines he mentions Christ many times. He keeps bringing up the one who was being set aside, and so imprints a longing for him on their souls.

Already he is showing them that the hope laid up for us, the hope of the resurrection and the kingdom, was not brought about by the administration of angels, but by the coming of our Savior Jesus Christ.
By saying "in the word of truth" he shows that it is dangerous to disregard the gospel, since it is true and free of falsehood.

By adding "as also in the whole world" he strengthens their faith. "The gospel," he says, "has reached not only as far as you, but already into the whole world." This is a sign of the power of Christ at work in the preaching.
For it was not neglected. Instead it bears fruit and grows.
The hope laid up for us, the hope of the resurrection and the kingdom, was not brought about by the administration of angels, but by the coming of Jesus Christ.

"And the gospel that has come to you," he says, "is not a falsehood that may be disregarded. Nor has it reached you alone; it has reached all people. And it did not reach them only to be ignored. It is bearing fruit and growing."
He commends Epaphras as one of the saints and as the one who would instruct them, so that they would pay more attention to his teaching.

What was the will of God? That you should recognize and know that you cannot be saved through angels, but only through Jesus Christ. How then shall we come to know this? In spiritual wisdom, not worldly wisdom.

He did especially well to add patience to endurance. Endurance cannot stand without patience, and endurance without joy has no reward. Joy above all is needed in these things. It is not the one who grieves over afflictions suffered for Christ who receives the reward from God, but the one who rejoices in them. And what is the reward? Adoption as sons, the inheritance, and life in the company of angels.

Before the flood and after the flood, before the law and under the law, the angels served God for your salvation. Yet God did not transfer us into his kingdom then. Now, however, his kingdom has been granted to us through our Lord, his Only-begotten. As for "the Son of his love": this does not mean that Christ is the son of God's love. Some are called sons of disobedience, others sons of Gehenna, and the devil is called the son of perdition. A person is named the son of whatever he has run to and attached himself to. He is not a son by nature, but by kinship of character. In the same way the Savior was called the Son of God's love, because he is the Son of God not only by nature but also by the genuineness of love: "For the Father loves the Son," it says, "and has given all things into his hands." Or else it is because he loved us and suffered for us. It should be read like this: "into the kingdom of the love of his Son."

Before the flood and after the flood, before the law and under the law, there were angels serving God for our salvation, but they accomplished nothing. Now, however, God has transferred us into his kingdom through the Lord's dispensation. "Whom he loved": God loves the angels as ministers, but Christ as his Son. So he did not bring you into the kingdom of the angels, but into the kingdom of the Son of his love. We are under the heir, not under the household servants. He says "Son of love," then, because he is loved as a son, not because he is the offspring of God's love. The sons of disobedience are not sons of it by nature, the sons of Gehenna are not its children, the devil is not by nature a son of perdition, and the adversary is not a son of sin. In the same way, the Lord is not a son of love in that sense. But since the angels are servants who are loved, while the Son is loved as a son, he said "of the Son of his love." Or it can be read this way: "he transferred us into the kingdom of the love of his Son." The Son loved us and suffered for us in order to make us worthy of his kingdom, and that is why he says: "he transferred us into the kingdom of his Son." In loving sinners and doing them good he is exactly like the one who begot him, and so he is the image of the Father.

He means that he existed beforehand. If he did not exist before all things, how are all things created in him? He said that all things are created in him so that we would stop hoping in angels and put our hope in Christ. "In him" means "through him." These things are said to the Jews, so that they would not think he existed only from the time he came to be among them in a body. "All things have been created through him and for him." This means that the cause of creation goes back to him. Or he said "for him" because nothing created lies outside him, and all things are encompassed by him. "And all things hold together in him": that is, through him. Or it means that by his will and power he holds all things together, according to the mystery hidden in God, who created all things.

To show you that he is before all things, he said that he was born "firstborn of all creation." He shows this still more clearly by what follows, when he says that "in him all things were created." If he were not before all things, how could all things have been created in him? So "firstborn" is not used in its strict sense, since in that sense it would contradict "only-begotten." By nature, the only-begotten is the one who is his father's only child, while the firstborn is the one who has other brothers and is the first of them. Both terms cannot be taken in their strict sense. He said that all things were created in him so that we would stop hoping in angels and place our hopes in Christ. This is why Paul speaks of his divinity and shows him to be the creator of all creation. "In him" is used to mean "through him."

He called him firstborn of all creation because he existed before creation. In the same way he calls him firstborn from the dead because he rose to incorruption before the other dead. No one would say that when the dead rise they will all be Christ's brothers, and that is why it was said with reference to the end, since most of them are sinners and ungodly. So in the passage before us, as here too, the notion of time is redundant.

"That in all things he might be preeminent." In which things? In those of the dispensation. He is first in obedience, first in baptism, first in his way of life, first in suffering, first from the dead. So he is rightly preeminent in all things, since he has become the beginning for those who follow.
"And he is the head of the body, the church." He is the creator of creation, and also the creator of our conversion.

"That in all things he himself might be preeminent." He is head of the church and firstborn from the dead. He is first in his way of life, first in sufferings, first in obedience, and first in baptism. So in all things he is preeminent in the dispensation.

This connects with "he is the head of the church." He has called the church the "fullness," as he has already rightly said, because it has been filled with the Holy Spirit. He says that Christ was pleased for all the fullness to dwell in him, and so through himself to reconcile all things and unite them to himself.

In the Letter to the Ephesians he showed that the church is called the fullness of God. So God was pleased for his fullness, that is, the church filled by him, to dwell in Christ as in its own head. This means that it keeps in step with him and depends on him, not on angels. He was pleased to reconcile all things through him, not through angels. Indeed, all that has been accomplished for the world has been accomplished through Christ.
By such words he teaches them that it is not angels who will reconcile them to God, but the Son. For he says: "he reconciled us in the body of his flesh."
The gospel has reached not only as far as you but the whole inhabited world. Yet nowhere has anyone been moved from it; all remain steadfast. So you too must stand firm now.

"If there is anything lacking in my sufferings," he says, "then I am filling up what remains of the afflictions for Christ's sake, and I rejoice to suffer on your behalf." Why on your behalf? Because he suffered for preaching to them.

If Christ is the head of the body, the church, then the afflictions brought on the church by those who rise up against the word of truth are quite rightly called Christ's afflictions. Anyone who distinguishes himself and contends in these afflictions may fittingly say that he is filling up in turn what is lacking in Christ's afflictions.

The mystery is the dispensation and incarnation of Christ. The glory of the mystery is the resurrection from the dead. The riches are the great mercy that comes from the forgiveness given in baptism, which grants rebirth to those who are baptized. What are the riches of the glory of this mystery? "Do not become poor," he says, "by running for refuge to the patronage of angels."
"Christ," he says, "has been given to us as our riches. Let us not become poor by turning to the patronage of angels."
If the hidden treasures of knowledge are in Christ, then clearly we share in them through Christ himself, not through angels.

Walking may seem to be the opposite of being rooted, but in this passage they are not opposites. Being rooted shows all of us the steadfastness of faith. Walking in Christ means plainly following in Christ's footsteps by living the same way of life.

He means the church, since it has been filled with the divinity of the Father. The sense is this: the church is full, and it dwells in Christ bodily, that is, as a body united to its head. Everywhere he calls Christ the head of the church. "And you have been filled in him" means "filled through him." Filled with what? Clearly with the Holy Spirit. "Who is the head of all rule and authority." "He is head not only of the church," he says (for that belongs specifically to the dispensation), "but also of every invisible power, since he is also its creator."

He means the church, which has been filled by his divinity, as he says elsewhere: "of him who fills all in all." Here "bodily" means as a body is in its head. Why, then, did he not add "which is the church"?

That is, he circumcised us from the sin of the flesh through baptism and made us alive to himself. So baptism in Christ is a spiritual circumcision, because it cuts away the sins of those who believe.

For it is through baptism that sins are removed and circumcised. "Buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him." Those who are baptized in the blood of Christ confess through baptism that they share in his death. Since they have shared in his death, it follows that they will also enjoy his resurrection. Resurrection is spoken of in two ways: one is spiritual, the other bodily. All human flesh will rise because of Christ's resurrection from the dead. But those who were not baptized in Christ and died in their unbelief will share in the common resurrection without enjoying the redemption and the promise. Those who were baptized into Christ, however, have freely gained another resurrection even before the common one, because they have already risen from the death of sins. That is why he said "in which you were also raised," not "in which you will be raised." How, then, can those who have been raised from the death of sins go on living as people who will die again? Would they not have risen in vain? But if they live as people who will live forever, then they do not live according to the flesh, enslaved to its desires. Instead they will live according to the Spirit. By "the body of sin" he means wicked deeds, because these are carried out through the body. So baptism is the circumcision of Christ, because it removes the body of sin, the foreskin. Just as the foreskin is something superfluous to a Jew, so sin is superfluous to soul and body. He kept to the figure throughout. By "the foreskin of the flesh" he means sin.

When the law that curses transgressors was given, all the people of Israel stood and shouted. They assented to what was said and accepted it, and their assent became like a bond. Christ blotted out this bond, the assent to the law, by his own decrees. He issued decrees against the observances of the law. About foods, he declared that it is not what goes into a person but what comes out that defiles. About sabbath-keeping, he healed on the sabbath. Anyone who looks will find many other such things. So above all he abolished the law's punishments against sinners by his decrees concerning sin [?], granting forgiveness of sins and repentance leading to salvation. And since the people said "Amen" to the curses, the bond was put in place as one that had been signed.

"Having stripped off the rulers and authorities, he made a public example of them, triumphing on the cross." By stripping off and laying aside the flesh he brought down the hostile powers. So "having stripped off the rulers and authorities he made a public example of them, triumphing over them in it." Until the cross and his very death it remained hidden that our Lord was both God and the Son of God. He amazed people with his miracles, but he was veiled by his body. That is why Satan tempted him. He wanted to learn whether he was the one proclaimed by the prophets, so that if he found out, he could obstruct the dispensation. But the evil one achieved nothing, since he could not find out, and for the time being Christ remained hidden. But once he had been nailed to the cross, had died, been buried and risen, and had fulfilled the whole dispensation, he stripped off his concealment. With head uncovered he showed his divinity, present with his body, for all to see. The first work of God was the resurrection from the dead, then the ascent into heaven, then the power at work in his name through his ministers and the other saints. So having stripped off his concealment, he openly made a public example of the hostile authorities. And what was this public exposure? That they have become weaker than human beings, that they are trampled underfoot, and that people mock them in the name of the Lord. Others have taken "having stripped off" to mean "having stripped them."

How did he blot out the bond that stood against us? When the law that curses transgressors was given, all the people of Israel cried out, accepting it and agreeing to it. So their assent became like a bond. He blotted out this bond by his decrees. Which decrees? Those that set us free from the way of life under the law and give us the way of life under grace.

He lived his life on our behalf, undoing disobedience and removing sin. He was offered up and bore our sins. By destroying these he brought down the devil's power. "Having stripped off, he made a public example" is put in place of "having stripped the rulers and authorities." Through this stripping he triumphed over the hostile powers and exposed them. So in himself he stripped them off, and he triumphed over them through what he suffered and accomplished.

"Therefore let no one judge you." He teaches that the law has been abolished, since Christ has blotted out the bond that stood against us. He also teaches that the evil one has fallen, since the Lord has stripped off the rulers and authorities and made a public example of them. So he commands them not to obey any longer these things, which have been abolished by Christ's working. "So do not submit to the Jews," he says, "who try to persuade you to keep what is in the law." Those things were a shadow of the body of Christ, which is the church. A shadow runs ahead of the body, but has no substance of its own. Therefore he says: do not obey the law. "Nor should you submit to the Greeks, who would lead you over to worshiping angels or the elements of this world." For they intrude into things they have not seen, being [?] by their own mind and their own reasoning. So "let no one judge you" is said about the Jews, and "let no one disqualify you" about the Greeks. He means: let no one plot against you, now that you are already winning and overcoming the evil one.

"Which are a shadow of things to come, but the body belongs to Christ." "When these things took place," he says, "they were a shadow of things to come." A shadow runs ahead of the body. Since the ordinances of the law are the shadow, what is the body? The things of Christ, which are no shadow. So now that the body has come, the shadow is superfluous.

What humility does he mean? Their saying: "We are lowly, but God is great and beyond being served by us. Since we cannot reach as far as him, we appease him through his angels and are brought near to him through them." Earlier he said: "who is the head of all rule and authority." Now he says: why do you go to the elements and the angels, having abandoned their head, who is Christ?

They said that God is great, incomprehensible and invisible, and that we cannot reach that far. "Therefore," they said, "since we cannot take in the Great One, we are brought near through angels." This is what he calls humility.

Here he revealed the aim we have been describing: he was moved to write because some people were urging others to be brought near to God through angels. "We must hold fast to the head," he says, for God the Word is the head of all. Why, then, do you let go of the head and cling to the body? For even if it has the role of a joint connecting [?]

…two members or more, the power of the angels. Yet the benefit comes from the head to all: to angels as angels, to archangels as archangels, to visible things as visible things. Suppose with me that heaven stands in place of a head for the world, and the sun and moon in place of eyes; and if you arrange each part of the world in the order of members in this way, you will find one body of the universe. And just as the soul is in the body and the body belongs to the soul, so the invisible powers are in the visible things. But more sovereign than all of these is the head, from which the benefit comes to the whole body, supplied, that is, from the head.

If you died with Christ for this reason, he says, so as neither to worship the elements of this world nor to live as its citizens, why do you put up with those who lay down rules for you according to this world's way of life, as though you lived by it? Why, as though you were living in the world, do you submit to regulations: "Do not taste, do not touch, do not handle," things that all perish as they are used? He sets these out as pagan doctrines, for in their own error these people command that one neither touch nor taste anything that has a soul. Yet all these things were given to human beings for consumption, that is, to be destroyed and used up in the use and demands of life. So, "Do not touch" the things God has given: according to their commandments and their teachings.

That is: beware of these things, I mean "do not touch, do not taste, do not handle," which seem to have some rationale, since it is the mark of the humble-minded and of those who do not spare the body to abstain from foods and not to honour their own flesh by filling it. But even if abstinence as such is good, the second point is impious. For they abstain not only as people who have mastered the belly, but also on the ground that they must not wrong living creatures, which were given to be consumed in the use of life. And so they want to be more merciful toward irrational animals than God is.
"Our life is hidden": that is, the blessedness of eternal life, which will be revealed to all when the glory of Christ is also revealed at his second coming.
Just as he often calls sin "flesh," so now too, listing the members of the flesh, he names fornication and impurity and the rest; for these are the members of sin.
By "the old man" he means the mind-set of sin, and by its members, evil deeds; by "the new man" he means the spiritual mind-set, and by its members, good deeds.

He calls sin "flesh," and he also lists its members. Having listed the man made up of these members, he urges us to strip off the old man with his deeds. So the old man is the mind-set of sin, and his members are sinful deeds. And just as there is an old man, so there is also a new one, that is, the spiritual mind-set; and its members are good deeds, which he also lists when he says "kindness, patience," and the rest.

This is like "that all may be in all." What he means is this: that in all who set their minds on the things of God, God may work all things. For when you think and do the things of Christ, he is the one acting through you, and he is in you.

It is like "that God may be all in all": not heaven in heaven, nor earth in earth. What he means is this: when you think and do his things, God is the one acting through you, and he is in you by your doing what pleases him.
Unless love leads the way, nothing that ought to be done is brought to completion. For it is when we love one another that we refrain from doing each other harm and take care to do each other good.

Do not let those who lead you astray, he says, act as umpires against you; rather let the peace of Christ be umpire within you, so that you are united to Christ. "And be thankful." To whom? Clearly to the one who called you,
Christ; and do not go fawning on angels.

Do not let those who lead you astray act as umpires against you, but let the peace of Christ be umpire in your hearts, that is, by your being united to Christ and setting your minds on his things. Then comes another exhortation.
When your slaves, he says, serve you with goodwill, you masters must also repay them justly and fairly with fitting care. So the fairness is to match their goodwill.

The Christians in Thessalonica, who had come to faith from among the Gentiles, endured many persecutions from those who were still pagans, and he consoles them for these. He also speaks of the resurrection of the dead, consoling them over the loss of their own people. The thanksgiving to God placed at the head of the opening is a testimony to the Thessalonians' piety.
Faith rouses one to the work of what is good; love makes one persist in labours; and hope makes those who struggle endure with patience.
Faith rouses one to toil, and love makes one persevere in labours.

Knowing, he says, beloved brothers, that the gospel did not come to you in word only, but also in power. Not only did we preach the word to you, he says, but we also displayed mighty works and miracles to you.
That is, it is spread abroad and loudly proclaimed.
The evils at Philippi, he says, did not take away our boldness for Christ; on the contrary, when we came to you we preached the word fearlessly.
The gospel by which we encourage the afflicted, that is, the resurrection and the reward given in it, is preached not out of error but in truth.
That is, burdensome and oppressive, by demanding the honours with which apostles of Christ ought to be honoured.

He did not say "that no one give way," so as not to seem to accuse them; instead he chose a word that cannot be taken as a reproach for slackness, saying "be shaken," that is, that no one should be thrown off balance.
He himself was not going to be left behind, he says; rather, "we" means either that those left will be so few and

easily counted that they will not precede the saints who have fallen asleep in going to meet Christ. For even if all are raised, not all will meet Christ, but only the righteous. It is clear, then, that at Christ's coming some are also found still alive. Or else what he says is something like this: if Christ were to come now, we who are left today would not precede those who have fallen asleep at Christ's coming. The pause should be placed after "those who are left": "until the day of the Lord we shall not precede those who have fallen asleep." "With the voice of an archangel." The Lord says the same: "At midnight there was a cry: Look, the bridegroom is coming!" "And the dead in Christ will rise first." This again the Lord himself says in the Gospels, and from this both the Lord and the apostle hint that the Lord's coming will be at night. "Then we who are alive, who are left": that is, the righteous of our kind.
He means that some will be found still alive at Christ's coming, and that this is shown

by "we who are left at the coming of the Lord." And this is like what the Saviour says: "For as in the days of Noah they were marrying and being given in marriage, and suddenly the flood came and took them all, so will the coming of the Son of Man be." So, he says, some are found alive.

"With a command and with the voice of an archangel, and the dead in Christ will rise." The Lord himself says this in the Gospel: "At midnight," he says, "there was a cry: The bridegroom is coming!" And that some are found alive, who are also taken up together with those who have fallen asleep, the Lord makes clear in the Gospel when he says: "Two will be in one bed; one will be taken and the other left. And two women will be grinding; one will be taken and the other left." Both the Lord and Paul hint that the coming will be at night.

By "the day of the Lord" he means his coming. He compared it to a thief because it comes unnoticed and unexpectedly; and "in the night," because when the day arrives it exposes the evil deeds done in the night.

But the bride, the soul adorned with the adornment of the virtues, sleeping the sleep of the day, which has no share in night and is yoked to wakefulness, said quite fittingly: "I sleep, but my heart is awake." That is why, though she slept in this way, the voice of the bridegroom did not escape her; she perceived him knocking at the door and said: "The voice of my beloved knocks at the door."
That is, not among those who are condemned, but among those who are saved.

That is why he says: Christ died for us so that, whether we wake, that is, live, or sleep, that is, die (for here he has taken "sleep" in a different sense from above), we may live together with him. For those who have acquired the armour he has described will live and reign together with Christ.

The Spirit is quenched when one's conduct is unworthy of the faith. "Do not despise prophecies. Test everything." Do not, he says, set traps for the hidden revelations of the Spirit, nor accept every announcement without testing it.

Nowhere has he set down these three, spirit, soul and body, in the case of an unbeliever, but only in the case of believers. Their soul and body belong to nature, but the spirit belongs to the divine favour, that is, it is the gift of grace given to believers. And he did not say "may they be kept blameless," lest you think he is praying for the gifts, but "blamelessly," that is, as we live blamelessly and preserve them through piety.

Again he consoles the Thessalonians for the persecutions they were enduring, recalling from the very opening the just and great recompense of Christ, which punishes the wicked and crowns the saints. Then, since there was much inquiry about Christ's second coming, as to when he will come, he corrects their assumptions on this point too, so that they would not be caught off guard or carried away by strange teachings. He sets out both the manner and the order of events of Christ's coming, which will take place again after the deception of the Antichrist.
Love joined with justice means not only loving but also being loved in return.

"If indeed it is just" is not an expression of doubt but of emphasis and affirmation; for it is said as a figure of speech, as we often say when it is day, "if indeed it is day." "Giving vengeance to those who do not know God": that is, bringing punishment on the ungodly. "With the angels of his power in flaming fire." Through these words he sets forth the terror of the glorious coming, and also through what he adds to encourage those who have been wronged; for a great consolation is not only the reward for one's sufferings but also the punishment inflicted on those who wronged them.
"Because our testimony was believed" on that day: for faith here prepares the reward in advance for that day. Which day? The day on which Christ will come.

He urges them not to be thrown into untimely alarm before the Lord's appearing: not if people in whom there is a spirit of error claim to be prophets, nor if words and rumours about the Lord are spread abroad, nor if some forge a letter and bring it as though it were ours. For unless the apostasy comes first and the man of sin is revealed, the son of perdition, who opposes and

exalts himself above every so-called god or object of worship. Do not expect the Saviour, he says, before the deceiver, who must come first, as I said. "Exalting himself above every god or object of worship": that is, above all idolatry. For just as he himself established it, so he himself will overturn it when he comes, along with every heresy he set up against the word of truth, so that people may be condemned on this count too: that the idols by which they were led astray were torn down not by themselves but by the one who led them astray. The devil established these errors from the beginning, drawing people away from God little by little and quietly introducing worship of himself in its place, so that when he comes afterward he may easily bring them under himself, since they have been led astray and are outside God's help. The Saviour himself also foretold this future deception of humankind, saying that when he comes it will be hard for him to find faith on the earth. "The man of sin" is the Antichrist; for he will come to Jerusalem as if to rebuild the temple, and will stand in the holy place proclaiming himself God. "Who opposes and exalts himself above every so-called god": that is, above all idolatry; "and above every object of worship": that is, above every

heresy that he set up against the word of truth. Like the scaffolding under an arch, so the heresies among those called both Jews and Greeks are a preparation for the devil. And just as, once the arch has been locked tight and has taken its proper shape, the scaffolding is dismantled and the arch alone remains standing firm, so the devil laid down the many heresies and paths of error as scaffolding, building up his own worship like an arch.

By this he shows that the idolatry the devil established, he himself overturns when he comes. And every heresy he set up against the word of truth, he himself dissolves when he comes, so that in this too people may incur judgment: that the things by which they were led astray were torn down not by themselves but by the one who led them astray. For the devil put these errors together piece by piece, drawing people away from God and quietly introducing worship of himself in its place, so that when he comes afterward and finds everything prepared in advance, with people led astray and outside God's help, he may think he can easily achieve what he is striving for, namely, to be worshipped by all people.

For like the scaffolding under an arch, so are the heresies, both those among the Greeks and those among the Christians, to the devil. And just as, once the arch has been locked tight and has taken its proper shape, the scaffolding is removed and the arch alone remains standing firm, so the devil laid down the many heresies and paths of error as scaffolding, preparing his own worship beforehand like a very great arch, so that when he comes, taking vengeance on all the heresies, he may himself abolish them, bringing people to the naked worship of himself.
In imitation of the Saviour, Satan comes in a complete human being.

The Holy Spirit restrains and hinders the coming of the lawless one. When, therefore, he says, this is taken out of the way and departs because of human wickedness, then the lawless one will have room to be revealed and to rise up, with no one hindering him. He said this because the mystery of lawlessness has already made a beginning, since in apostolic times both schisms and heresies arose, and from then on the devil has been working unbelief in people. For the mystery of ungodliness is already at work. Indeed the Manichaeans have already said that the devil is the God of the law, and Marcion said that the God of the law is not the Father of Christ, and some say they

worship the one who is greater than all. Mani also says that he himself is Christ, and that he himself is the Paraclete. "Only he who now restrains will do so until he is out of the way, and then the lawless one will be revealed." And the Holy Spirit restrains and hinders the coming of the lawless one, as he has already said. "And now you know what restrains."
By "what restrains" he means the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Isaiah also foretold this; for having spoken of the one from the root of Jesse, he added: "And he will strike the earth with the word of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he will slay the ungodly." And he foretold that he would strike the earth through the last of the prophets as well, who said: "For you who fear, the sun of righteousness will rise, with healing in its wings." And shortly after: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the Tishbite," and he added: "lest I come and strike the earth utterly."

"And he will destroy him by the manifestation of his coming." Christ is our life; so when Christ, our life, is revealed, he necessarily destroys the devil as well, the one who brought about death. And in imitation of the Saviour, Satan comes in a complete human being, whose coming is

according to the working of Satan, with all power and signs, and so on. In imitation of Christ's bodily sojourn, of his saving dispensation on our behalf, Satan comes and works in a human being, as I have already said.

This is "and with the breath of his lips he will slay the ungodly," which Isaiah says; for having spoken of the one from the root of Jesse, he added: "And he will strike the earth with the word of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he will slay the ungodly." And he foretold the striking of the earth through the last of the prophets as well: for having said, "For you who fear me the sun of righteousness will rise," and shortly after, "Behold, I send you Elijah the Tishbite," he added as his final word: "lest I come and strike the earth utterly."

"And he will destroy him by the manifestation of his coming." The apostle called Christ our life, and added: "when your life is revealed." So when life is revealed from heaven, it is impossible for the one who brought about death not to be destroyed, he whose coming is according to the working of Satan.

This ought to have convinced the Apollinarians and the Arians that God the Word assumed a whole human being. For in imitation of righteousness and of the saving dispensation on our behalf, Satan comes and will work in a human being.

He did not put "by command" in the other letters. Why does he put it now? Because he was about to lay down certain laws and set out the canons of the Church. He convinces them in advance that he is going to speak by God's command.

And yet the law also contains things to be done, and grace things to be forbidden; but he named each by what predominates in it, especially since under grace the Saviour's commandments are not laws but are left to free choice. If these are not carried out, the one who has not done them is not necessarily condemned: for example, the treasure of virginity, and anything else of that kind.

But perhaps someone will say: How can you say that the one who died is God, when Paul clearly said in what he wrote to Timothy, "the man Jesus Christ, who gave himself as a ransom for all"? What then? Do you not hear him saying that the Lord of glory was crucified? And that from Judah, according to the flesh, came Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever, amen? And that Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever? For he was one, from both divinity and humanity, each nature existing perfectly according to its own principle, being consubstantial with the Father according to his divinity and the same one consubstantial with us human beings according to his humanity. For indeed the human being as we know him, consisting of soul and body and making up one hypostasis, we call a mortal rational living being: mortal according to the body, rational according to the soul. Yet the whole living being is called mortal and the whole is called rational, and the elements of which it is naturally

composed are neither confused nor divided into two persons. So too Emmanuel, being one from two natures, one hypostasis and one incarnate nature of the Word himself, neither confused the elements from which the ineffable union came about, nor, remaining one, does he give an opening to duality, from which division comes. For what is properly one could never become two, and if it passed over into two it would wholly cease to be one. Since, then, Jesus Christ is one, even if someone names him from one part and calls him man, he is understood as God incarnate; and conversely, if one calls him God, the Word made man is signified. For this reason, knowing him to be one and undivided, we necessarily use the qualification, saying that he is consubstantial with the Father according to his divinity and the same one consubstantial with us according to his humanity, and the same one passible in the flesh and impassible in the divinity. In the same way one can see the divinely inspired Scripture setting this out as well: in one place Christ is said to have been handed over by the Father, in another he is written to have handed himself over. Writing to the Romans, Paul says of the Father: "He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all." And to Timothy he writes this: "There is one God, and a mediator between God and humans, the man Jesus Christ, who gave himself as a ransom for all." And observe with me how polished and precise Scripture is. Where he called Christ the own Son of God the Father and said, "he who did not spare his own Son," showing that "own" means the one who is of the same essence and not alien, he then added the lowly, economic phrase, "handed him over for us all." But where he put the economic first and said, "the man Jesus Christ," he added what befits God, and did not say "who was handed over" but "who gave himself as a ransom for all." And writing to the Galatians he says this: "The life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and handed himself over for me." Why, then, do the children of Nestorius pass over things said with such consummate skill and in a harmony wholly befitting God, and, clinging to Jewish blindness and pettiness, bring forward that Christ was handed over or raised by the Father, trying to use these, as they suppose, to show that he is not true God after he truly became man?
Since this woman fell into transgression, she will be saved through the children who will be born to her and the descendants who will accomplish the

…piety. What then, if she has no children, or has children but not sons? Even if children are born to only some women, they are born for the whole race; and that is why the transgression is spoken of as belonging to the female sex as a whole. For if one woman is the cause of evil for all, how is it not reasonable that the many, by bearing godly children, should undo the evil that one woman brought upon them, since Christ has made the beginning of that undoing through himself? From what, then, will the woman be saved? From the transgression and the disobedience. So she must also have good deeds of her own, so that once the disobedience is forgiven, her other sins may not condemn her. He did not say “she will be saved through childbearing” without purpose. He said it so that mothers, whose salvation depends on their children, may bring them up in all piety and righteousness. And as for being saved through childbearing: the woman is not judged by the things in which she transgressed. She will be saved through those things by which she becomes the mother of the obedient, that is, on the principle of obedience, since she also has her own good deeds through which she is saved. As we said before, he says this so that mothers may bring up their children in piety.
She will be saved from the reproach of the transgression through childbearing. The apostle says this not to reproach her, but to urge her toward piety and toward bringing up her children in faith.

He did not say “an honor” or “a bodyguard of attendants,” but “a good work,” meaning a good course, a good labor, because of the oversight of the churches. “If anyone aspires to the office of bishop, he desires a good work.” He made a concession, not to the aspiring but to the effort, so that a person might train himself to become fit for the office of bishop. Or rather, his allowing the aspiration is an encouragement to a good life. It becomes a kind of approach to doing good and to the finest life. So while he seems to have allowed the desire, by what he goes on to say he urges them on all the more.

He made a concession to the aspiration, not to the effort, so that a person might prepare himself through good works and faith to become fit for the office of bishop. So his allowing the aspiration is rather an encouragement to a good life. The aspiration is a kind of entrance into doing good and into the finest life. He lists so many qualities that must belong to the bishop that they are enough to deter rather than attract. So while he seems to have allowed the desire, by listing what sort of man the bishop must be he deters all the more.
He gives his exhortation in the most instructive way, setting out one by one the features of a blameless way of life.
The striker is not the one who rebukes, but the one who is carried away without reason. A just charge brings shame, but an unreasonable reproach wounds.

That is, he was seen in the flesh, but he was justified in the Spirit because he lived by the Spirit. Even though he was in the flesh, he did not live according to the flesh. He subjected the flesh to the Spirit and opened up for us the way of righteousness. Or he may also mean that, as the Spirit worked signs, Christ was justified in keeping with our confession and faith. “Seen by angels.” Who? The crucified Christ. He does not say this because the angels do not see his divinity, for the Savior himself said that the angels see the face of “my Father in heaven.” When it says, “No one has ever seen God,” it clearly means that no one has seen him as he is, but only as far as an angel or a human being is able to see. God, then, is invisible to both angels and human beings, but he was seen through the dispensation.

The church on earth was justified in the Spirit through its confession. This is like “that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.” For as the Spirit worked the signs, he was justified in keeping with our confession and the faith of those who believe. He who came for the salvation of human beings was seen by angels. By this he showed that the divinity of the Only-begotten is invisible even to angels, but that he was seen by them through the flesh. “Taken up in glory,” that is, on the clouds.
That is, if after being widowed she did not cast off the children she had.
“If she has shown hospitality,” that is, to believers, and even while she was still counted as married.
“If she has washed the feet of the saints.” He added this to show that they must also be received with care. It is clear that he requires these things too
only according to her means when he says all this, for she is not poorer than the woman who put in the two obols.

Because, after promising Christ to remain as they were, they later married. By “first faith” he means their first pledge of submission. Or again, “first” means what was foremost for them, the highest and most supreme of all.
Teaching is the simple handing on of Scripture through its words and the explanation of the meanings contained in those words. “Word” is what presents those meanings.

Since he said above, “Do not lay hands on anyone hastily, and do not share in other people's sins,” he now gives the reason he said it. Not everyone's sins are evident, for many people sin in secret. So he says: test them over time, for what could escape notice today is exposed tomorrow. Some sins are evident and go before them to people's judgment, since everyone knows that such people sin and judges them unworthy. Others come to light afterward, and those that are otherwise cannot stay hidden. Since this is how things stand with people, do not lay hands on anyone hastily. Otherwise he may turn out to be sinning in secret and be promoted though unworthy, and you will share in his fault.

“Likewise good works are also evident.” About good works he said only that they cannot stay hidden. He did not say that they escape notice. About evil works, however, he said that some are evident and some escape notice. Why? Because no one is quick to hide what is good. “He who does the truth comes to the light,” but the evildoer hides because he wants to escape notice.
The devout and believing master is quick to accept the slave's good service and goodwill, and being kind, he becomes grateful to him.
On “those who partake of the benefit”: that is, those who are sensitive to it and ready to repay it.
Just as fire is produced when stone and wood rub together, so impiety is born when the wicked gather together.

He does not say “who gives life” without purpose. He says it to remind us that the one who gives life and grants each person a return to life will also give each a fitting reward at the time of the resurrection. He said it because he was about to command him to keep the faith.

He did not use this expression without purpose. If God gives life to all things, he will clearly count the godly worthy of the resurrection as well, beyond the life he gives to all, granting a return to life to bodies that die. So, since he is about to charge him to keep the commandment spotless, he mentions the one who gives life, so that the hope of that future life may urge him toward piety. Note that when he says “who gives life to all things,” he does not mean that we should think God gives life even to lifeless things. The same applies to “All things were made through him”: it does not mean absolutely all things, but those under discussion.

For created beings remain in immortality and incorruption by his grace and will and need to share in him, even if they were given an immortal nature, as the angels were. Immortality belongs properly to him alone, since he is life itself, what holds all beings in existence, and the giver of every good.

In the first letter, since he was about to hand down rules for the church, he said “by command.” In the second he said “according to the promise.” For his apostleship, on the one hand, sets in order what is beneficial by God's command. On the other hand, it offers its hearers the promise of life, not the present life but the eternal life that is in Christ Jesus.
