In the first letter he says “by command,” since he is about to give instructions. In the second letter he says “according to the promise.” For the apostleship does give instructions, but in the hope that those who obey will obtain eternal life.
He is not speaking of an unbroken record in his life, but of his faith in God.

The trials brought against those who preached the gospel were hindering the gospel, and that is why he says, “Share in suffering for the gospel.” He added, “by the power of God,” because suffering itself needs God's help. God “abolished death and brought life and incorruption to light through the gospel.” There was life in Adam's time and for those after him, but it was darkened by the death that came from disobedience. Now it has been brought to light by Christ's resurrection: it was darkened by death, and it is brought to light through Christ.

How can the gospel be put to the test? In the way its preachers were put to the test. Since the trials brought against those who preached the gospel were hindering the gospel, that is why he says these things. — “And brought life to light.” What already exists is what is brought to light. Life was given before Adam's disobedience, but it was darkened by death. So by the Savior's resurrection life is brought to light again.
What deposit? The sound teaching he had taught him.

He had said earlier, “No soldier gets entangled in the affairs of everyday life.” That raised the question of how someone who avoids such entanglements will get what he needs. So he made it clear that one must live from the gospel.
Gangrene is a disease that rots the body and spreads through it easily.

He does not solemnly charge him because he condemns him for negligence. He does it so that, by this charge, he may keep his resolve firm to the end. “I solemnly charge you before God and the Lord Jesus Christ, who is to judge the living and the dead, by his appearing and his kingdom” means: so that when the Son of Man comes, I may have this defense, that I told you. He says this to give him boldness to preach the word.

By this command he wants the teacher to watch over his disciples at every season. “In season” refers to the reminder given after a sin, since that seems to be the right moment to rebuke someone who has sinned. But waiting until a person has sinned before rebuking him and turning him to repentance falls outside the help that prevents sin. So he corrects his statement and says, not only “in season” but also “out of season.” “Out of season” means before the sin is carried out. Most people think it unnecessary and untimely to speak to those who have not yet gone wrong. Yet to those who know how to judge, this “unnecessary” and “untimely” speaking is very necessary and timely. One must speak about fornication even to someone who is chaste, so that he does not fall into the nets of passion. To someone who values contentment and fairness it is right and fitting to set out the warnings against greed and the love of money, so that he does not
somehow, being off his guard, take in a shoot from the root of evils. For “the love of money is the root of all evils.” Paul the apostle laid this down.

“Fully carrying out” the ministry means fully and completely discharging everything that properly belongs to the high-priestly office. It also means supplying in every way the needs of the rational flock, so that it is complete in all its members, both priests and ministers. Those who have been given the dignity of the episcopate were appointed to build up and to plant, even if they must suffer hardship for it. That is why, in the words quoted, the apostle put enduring hardship before the work. He said, “Endure hardship, do the work of an evangelist.”
“I am being poured out”: that is, I am being put to death and slaughtered, so that my blood is sprinkled on the earth.

The poet who said, “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle bellies,” said it to rebuke them for wrongly pointing to a tomb of Zeus, a tomb that did not exist. Paul used the same line. So that he would not be thought to agree with the poet and to bear witness to the immortality of the so-called Zeus, he added, “This testimony is true.” That poet lied when he spoke up for Zeus, but I speak the truth when I say that the Cretans are always liars and idle bellies. This testimony is true, not that one.
He often teaches gentleness by praising it, but he found that the Cretans needed something like the goad of rebuke. That is why he said, “Rebuke them sharply.”
“To the pure all things are pure.” God made all things pure. If they are impure, the accusation reaches the one who created
them. And this is what is meant by “They profess to know God, but they deny him by their works.”
He showed that he is calling the women to a church office, for otherwise he would not have said “reverent as befits holy persons.”
He applied incorruptness [?] to the mind and dignity to conduct, so that a person may keep away not only from corrupt deeds but also from corrupt thoughts.

In many letters he uses an unusual expression to prepare for the argument he is about to introduce. Here too, since he was about to make a request on behalf of Onesimus on the strength of his own standing, and his standing lay in being in chains, he shows that his appeal deserves to be trusted.

The heretics say the letter is not Paul's. As their first proof they point out that his name is not placed at the beginning, as it is in the other letters. Their second proof is that the style is different, that is, foreign to Paul's, and so is the composition. It should be understood, then, that the Jews hated Paul for teaching apostasy from the law. That is why he was in danger in Jerusalem, barely escaped, and was sent to Rome. So when he wrote things that would benefit the Hebrews, he did not put his name first. He did not want their hatred of him to rob them of the benefit of the letter.

As the blessed Severian says, he wrote to them in the Hebrew language, and what he wrote was translated by one of his disciples, Luke, or more likely Clement, whom he also mentions. That is why the style is foreign. And

this question was examined by those before us. Eusebius, son of Pamphilus, who was more of a historian than those before or after him, mentioned the debate and said that our ancient fathers among the bishops held that the letter was Paul's.

“In many parts”: according to the different times in which God arranged his dealings with us, as in the creation of Adam, in the events concerning Cain, those concerning Noah, and those concerning Abraham, in the times before the law and after the law. For God's ordering of things on our behalf has many parts. “And in many ways”: because one commandment was given to Adam, another to Noah, another to Abraham, another through Moses, and various ones through the prophets.

“He has spoken to us in a Son” means “through a Son.” It is not “in him” as in an instrument, but “through him” as the one who took on flesh in the divine dispensation. Starting from this point, the Jews' understanding could take hold of the word, as if by touch, and so be led up to his existence before the ages. Having first said, “He has spoken to us in a Son, whom he also appointed heir,” where “appointed” means “made,” he raised the argument to the Son's existence before the ages. He does this constantly, at times rising to his divinity and at times coming down to his becoming human.

Wanting to show more clearly that the Word was begotten from the essence of the Father, he mentioned the radiance. Radiance comes from the essence of the thing whose radiance it is. It is continuous, it comes from that thing, and it is never conceived of apart from the thing whose radiance it is. But radiance suggests a nature lesser than the thing whose radiance it is, and it does not have its own hypostasis. So he made his meaning clear with another expression, saying, “and the exact imprint of his hypostasis.” He put the first phrase to show that the Son is from the essence without division, and the second to show that he is not without his own hypostasis. Just as John named him the Word and then added, “He was with God, and he was God,” so Paul said “radiance” and then added, “and the exact imprint of his hypostasis.”
This is what Jeremiah says: “Mighty are the works of his words.”

Even though the Word became flesh, he still remained in the glory and nature of the Godhead, and he did not leave the supreme thrones of God the Father. He was made a little lower than the angels because of the limits of humanity, since human nature ranks below the angels in glory. Even so, he was above every name that is named.

Just as with “radiance” and “imprint” he followed the thought of John, who called him the Word and said he was with God, so here too he follows John. John said, “He was in the beginning; all things were made through him,” meaning that he existed and these things did not. In the same way Paul says of the angels, “who makes,” but to the Son, “your throne.” He wants to show that what is made once did not exist, but the one who has an eternal throne was always with the Father.

He does not mean that their nature actually changes. He is speaking by comparison: these things are more likely to perish, and they all but perish when set beside the eternity of the Son. When the Lord foretold the second coming, he said that the stars would fall, but not the sun or the moon or the heaven.

“To which of the angels has he ever said?” He passes over the whole of creation and names what is higher than it, the angels. If the Son differs from the angels in that they came into being and he did not, how much more does he differ from all the invisible things? Note that through “But you are the same” he showed both that the Son's nature exists before the ages and that it does not change. And through saying, “Are they not all ministering spirits sent to serve?” he showed that the Son is not a minister but a co-worker.

He does not mean the law, but the word that was often delivered through angels. “It was confirmed to us by those who heard.” This is like the passage in the letter to the Galatians: “I went up because of a revelation and set before them the gospel, so that I might not be running, or have run, in vain.” It was confirmed not because we needed it, but because all the others were fully convinced that what I preach, I preach rightly.

He means the age to come. At the end he immediately added, “But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him; but we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels.” So he says that “What is man, that you remember him?” applies to Jesus, since what belongs to our common humanity applied to him. But the Son himself says, “Out of the mouths of infants and nursing babies you have perfected praise because of your enemies,” and “I will see the heavens, the works of your fingers.” No one would say that the man whom God remembered is the one who perfected praise out of the mouths of infants and nursing babies because of your enemies, and who says, “I will see the heavens, the works of your fingers.” This is the one who remembered the man and made him a little lower than the angels. And who is the man? Jesus, made a little lower than the angels because of the suffering of death.
He presents the present age as if it were a single day.
He speaks of a division of soul and spirit when the soul shares in the body's experiences while the grace of the Holy Spirit draws it back toward heavenly things.
Christ's starting point was Judaism, since he lived according to the law. That is why he says, “Leaving this behind, let us press on

to perfection,” knowing that the one who was to be a priest without the law had to be priest according to the order of Melchizedek. “From dead works, and of faith toward God, of baptisms.” To Christians, earthly things are dead. So, he says, it would be absurd to abandon this way of life, whether the life of faith or the life of having died to all things, and to go back again to the baptisms of the law. When the Lord came, he preached repentance, saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” This is repentance from dead works. So the phrase should be read as “of repentance from dead works,” meaning “of the repentance that turns away from dead works.” What he is saying is this: we must not abandon repentance from dead works, faith toward God, and baptism, and run back to the law. (He called baptism by a plural name because of the great number of people counted worthy of it. He mentioned baptisms, teaching, the laying on of hands by which ordinations take place, the hope of the resurrection, and so on.) He is preparing the ground for what follows. The priests under the law upheld the law, but Melchizedek was outside the law, and he who came was according to the order of Melchizedek. We must not, he says, abandon the priest according to the order of Melchizedek and uphold the priesthood under the law, so that the things of the law remain in force. He called the things of the law a foundation because they served humankind as a prelude to piety.

The apostles raised the dead, and this was the power of the resurrection. He said “holding him up to contempt” because, if baptism is a mystery, once is enough. If it is done a second time, it becomes contempt and public disgrace.

He took this as an illustration not of baptism, for how would it rule out a second baptism? Rather, he took it as an illustration of the power of the Holy Spirit, which grants its benefits again and again.

Having spoken above of the full assurance of hope, he showed that God gave Abraham assurance. This was not the assurance that comes through works and belongs to one's way of life, but the assurance that comes through God's dispensation.
Since God had sworn, it was impossible for him to change, and it was impossible for the power of the promise to be changed.

He does not mention without purpose how Melchizedek met Abraham after Abraham had defeated the Assyrians, and how Abraham gave him tithes of everything. He mentions it to show that the forefather of the Levitical tribe treated Melchizedek as a priest. Therefore the priesthood without the law is superior to the priesthood under the law.

“Without father, without mother, without genealogy” in respect of the priesthood. In the Levitical tribe it was evident whose child each person was, which priest's, or which priest's wife's. There were also fixed terms of priesthood. Some held yearly courses of service, while others served as priests for their whole lives. Both arrangements are found among the priests under the law, even if not in the same periods. He calls Melchizedek fatherless, motherless, and without genealogy, “having neither beginning of days nor end of life,” in respect of the priesthood. He had no priestly lineage. He did not begin at a set point by succeeding someone else. He did not succeed another priest through a course of service. Nor did he hold office under a law requiring him to be priest all his life. In short, everything said here is by comparison with the priests under the law. It is also said of Melchizedek, “but made like the Son of God, he remains a priest forever.” How does Melchizedek remain a priest? The statement poses a problem, and this is the solution. Just as Scripture calls the law “Moses,” so here “Melchizedek” sometimes means the man and sometimes the priesthood itself. If, then, Melchizedek has been made like the Son through the priesthood that is according to Christ, he remains forever. It is not the man who remains, for he was mortal, but the dignity of the priesthood.

Just as the tabernacle was built in the time of Moses so that the services of worship might be carried out, so this tabernacle is greater: the establishment of grace, the body of Christ, which has Christ as its head.
"By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning things to come." He put Jacob first and then Esau, not following the order of their birth but the order of the blessing.

"Of whom the world was not worthy." He does not say this about all of them, but about these last ones, whom he also recognizes as martyrs. He recalls those who put armies to flight and who received grace for the good of the people.

"Laying aside every weight." The weight is the sin of fleshly pleasure, from which is born the sin that so easily besets us. He called sin "easily besetting" because it readily surrounds us and leads us to do its will.
For the festal gathering and feast of the angels is the glory given to God, and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and to God the judge of all.
This is what Paul says elsewhere: "For the form of this world is passing away," so that temporary things may pass away and eternal things may come.
That is, those who are under the law do not have this gift in which we share. "Outside the camp" means outside the observances of the law and the camp of Israel.
